The sitting member for Beauharnois [DOT]was in the office of the notary, Mr. Johnston, who had not been seeu by anybody, very naturally from the moment on the 14th July preceding after he had fulfilled his part of the transaction was there, the notary was there and there was no1 money. What happened ? Through the interposition of Mr. Dandurand, the real estate agent chosen by the department to carry this transaction through, a note was discounted in the Sovereign Bank under the signature of Mr. Johnston without any credit that we could see attached to Mr. Johnston but on the representations made by Mr. Daudu-rand himself the personal note of Mr. Johnston with a bank with which he had never had any transaction whatever, was discounted for $10,000. The deed was then signed and the proceeds of the note were placed in the hands of the notary who was, as I have said, the agent both of the sitting member for Beauharnois as notary and as well the notary of the government. The notary handed over immediately the sum of $1,000 to the vendor and kept the balance to extinguish the mortgage of $4,500 and also to pay the amount of the accumulated interest which figured up I think to some $731. On the 18th, after having attended on behalf of the sitting member and on behalf also of the government to the discharge of this mortgage, Mr. Dunton, the notary, paid over the balance to the sitting member for Beauharnois, some $3,300. Now, the sale made by the sitting member to Mr. Johnston was for the sum of $10,000. but on the day when the sale, long suspended, was carried out, on the 1st December. Mr. Johnston seems to have reported to the sitting member that he was entitled to some $300. The evidence given by the sitting member is that the representation made to him by Mr. Johnston was that Mr. Johnston had trouble in negotiating to find the money. I assume, Sir, that we must give the sitting member credit for ordinary intelligence and he knew and knew positively, at that time that this Mr. Johnston had not in reality deeded this property over to the government that that part of the transaction had been decided weeks before ; yet, if we are to accept his statement upon the representation made by this man that he required $300, he abandoned to him this sum of $300, and the deed of sale instead of being for the sum of $10,000. the exact sum voted by parliament, the exact sum available and the only sum available for that purpose that year; the exact sum which is mentioned in the subsequent deed of sale by Johnston to the government, was for the sum 'of $9,700. How the sitting member could have accepted this statement that Mi-. Johnston notified to him in the official letter of the secretary of the Department of Public Works weeks previously as the man -who was selling this property to the government; how I say Mr. MONK.
the sitting member could have accepted this plea for the payment of $300 and accepted it upon the reasons alleged by Mr. Johnston, it is for the House to decide.
Now, Sir, this note for $10,000 was renewed. It was kept in the bank until further- pressure from some parties-whether acting on behalf of the sitting member or otherwise-until further pressure was brought to bear upon the government to issue an official cheque. That cheque was issued from the Auditor General, from the Department of Finance, and it was made payable to wrhom 7 It was made payable to Mr. R. B. Johnston and also to the order of the notary, Mr. Dunton, who was, I claim, the agent, the appointee, the chosen notary of the sitting member for Beauharnois as well as the notary also chosen by Mr. Dandurand, and finally designated specially by the Department of Justice to act for that department: in this affair. That cheque came to Montreal and on the day it arrived in Montreal, with the proceeds of that cheque, this note lying in the Sovereign Bank for over a month was taken up and Mr. Johnston signed his deed of sale to the gov-fernment. Now, Sir, it is apparent, I think, to the members of this House that Johnston never acted in this matter in any other capacity but as the agent of the government. It is clear from the documents produced and the evidence of Mr. Dandurand, that Mr. Dandurand was the agent directly named by the government, and that Mr. Johnston never for a single moment occupied any other position than that of sub-agent named by Mr. Dandurand to secure an option upon this' property. Therefore he had no interest in the transaction but that of a paid employee, and from the moment he returned to Montreal and handed over his option and made report to Mr. Dandurand that he had fulfilled the duty required of him, he was paid off and disappeai'ed from this transaction and never reappeared until the day when it became necessary-not to secure his intervention for any purpose relating to the completion of this transaction, not to treat with the government whose agent in reality he was as to the price, but merely to intervene in the notary's office to sign the authentic deed containing worjl for word all the stipulations contained in the previously signed deed between the sitting member for Beauharnois and this sub-agent himself. Sir, I do not wish to take up unduly the time of the House but it seems to me that the circumstances of this case disclose as clear an infraction of section 10 of chapter il of the Act relating to the independence of parliament as it would be possible to place before this House. Few cases I submit could be clearer. In matters of this kind as in many other matters with which members of the legal profession are familiar, where it is designed to evade the law, titles never pass directly ; it passes through the agency of interposed persons, and who

bears that characteristic more in the present instance than the man Johnston who acted throughout this transaction V As to the knowledge of the sitting member I say that it is impossible after the communications which passed between the member for Beauharnois (Mr. Loy) and the government itself, weeks before this sale was completed; it is impossible for members of this House to arrive at any other conclusion, than that, at the time the sale was made on the 1st of December, the sitting member for Beauharnois knew perfectly well what was the role filled and to be filled by Mr. Johnston in this matter. Mr. Speaker, I submit to you that the amendment which I have proposed is well founded, and I would repeat that it seems to me that in bringing this matter to the notice of the House I have fulfilled a duty of which not only the public but the members of this House themselves ought to be grateful in a certain sense and in a certain degree. There was a time Sir, speaking more particularly for my own province, when there was no law in reference to the independence of members who sat in the representative assembly. I venture to assert without fear of contradiction that since that time there has been a tendency to violate to a certain degree that cardinal principle of the absolute independence of the members of this House, without which this House would be reduced to a state of absolute inutility. Under these circumstances it seems to me that every effort made for the absolute restoration of that independence so essential to the proper working of our representative institutions, is a step taken in the right direction.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. I. TARTE (St. Mary's, Montreal).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I fee] that it is incumbent on me to answer the observations that have just been made by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). I gladly acquit him of any improper motives on this occasion. He has stated, and I for one accept his statement in toto, that he has been animated by the desire of fulfilling his duty. He has invited his colleagues to take his word and I take his word. I would have been very pleased however if he had extended to myself and to Mr. Loy the same treatment, and had accepted our word. Mr. Loy and I have both stated on our word of honour the transaction as it took place. Mr. Loy stated on his honour that he had no knowledge of the purpose for which that property was acquired by Mr. Johnston. 1 stated on my word of honour that Mr. Loy never approached me and that I have never approached him when he was a member of parliament in reference to this matter. This personal question settled, permit me to call attention to the wording of my hon. friend's indictment. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) states first.
That in 1898 Mr. Loy bad sold his property when he was not a member of parliament, to Mr. Archambault.
With that the House has no concern. We have nothing to do with transactions carried on by gentlemen before they are elected to this House. The indictment as far as the sitting member is concerned is as follows
That from the time the said George Loy . handed his said property to Archambault up to the day of the sale of said property to the Crown or government of Canada, he never ceased to be the proprietor of said property, and that at the time of the sale of said property on the 20th January, 1903, said Robert Brice Johnston was merely acting for and cn behalf of said Loy, who in said manner did indirectly sell his said property to the Crown or government of Canada.
This is a very serious charge. My hon. friend, on information that he had received, has made to the House a statement that when Mr. Johnston bought Mr. Loy's property, he, Johnston, was acting on behalf of Mr. Loy himself-that in point of fact Johnston had been appointed as the agent of Mr. Loy to sell his property to that department. This is the gist of the charge. I ask my hon. friend frjom Jacques Cartier whether he has substantiated that charge in any way whatever ? Has it been established by a tittle of evidence that Mr. Johnston was the agent of Mr. Loy ? Why, Mr. Loy and Mr. Johnston have stated under oath that they did not know each other. Johnston had never met Mr. Loy, and Mr. Loy did not know Johnston even by sight. The Department of Public Works did not know Johnston. As my hon. friend has just said, before taking his seat, Johnston acted as an agent for Mr. Dandurand. He was paid for his services, not by Mr. Loy, but by Dandurand himself. It is true, Mr. Loy consented to give him $300 of the price of sale ; but at that time Mr. Loy did not) know that Johnston had been acting for the government. Now, my hon. friend wTill be obliged to recognize that he has utterly failed to establish the real point of his statement, that is to say, that Johnston was acting on behalf of Mr. Loy. That is the only point with which the House is concerned. I will not discuss the law in the matter. I will not follow my hon. friend in the statement he has made that the law might involve Mr. Loy in trouble because the deed of sale was not passed immediately. The main fact is that Mr. Loy did not know Johnston. Johnston, then, did not act for Mr. Loy. It is in evidence that Johnston was employed by Mr. Dandurand. In what capacity did Dandurand act ? The letters that are in evidence show. When on a tour of inspection of the different works of the department I called at Valleyfield. Parliament had placed at the disposal of the department the sum of $10,000 to erect a public building there. It was then my duty to choose a site. I proceeded to the town, I found that a government site on which perhaps I might have cast my eyes was no longer available, as it had been rented by the Department of Railways and

Canals some time previous. There was no other government property which was tit for a public edifice. I made up my mind that the Loy site was the only one that was really fit, and I immediately instructed Mr. Dandurand, whom I knew very well, who is a trusted real estate agent in Montreal, to acquire immediately the Loy site. I was aware that I could not purchase Mr. Loy's property with his knowledge that the government was purchasing from him. 1 instructed Mr. Dandurand accordingly. Not to awaken a suspicion, he appointed a sub-agent. That sub-agent went to Mr. L*y, represented to him that he wanted the property for commercial purposes, and took an option on the 14th of July. On the 16th of July the option was completed in Montreal, $100 being paid down as a guarantee of good faith, the deed to be passed later on. From that date Mr. Loy was no longer the owner of his former property. He had nothing more to do with it. He had pledged himself to sell, and practically had sold. Every man of business will agree that when a man has given an option on a property, lie is no longer the owner of that property, but has sold it. The deed had to be executed ; that was all that had to be done. My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier lays a good deal of stress on the fact that in the month of September, before the final deed of sale was executed, Mr. Loy was communicated with by the secretary of the Department of Public Works. I was away then. Mr. Dandurand, the government agent, had communicated to the department officially the fact that he had secured the property that was indicated to him. Let the House not lose sight of this fact, that in the month of August, before these communications took place between the department and Mr. Loy, Mr. Dandurand had officially notified the department that he had secured the property he had been instructed to secure. There is written evidence in the record of that fact. Then the department was officially acquainted with the fact that the property was ours. There was only the ordinary procedure to be followed, and that is just what was followed. When the department is notified that a site has been secured, before passing the deed, the department sends an official to ascertain whether the site has been rightly chosen, and whether the price agreed upon is not too high. That is just what was done in this case. Mr. Routhier, an architect of the Department of Public Works, proceeded to the town of Valleyfield, and carried out the procedure which I have just indicated, and it was to give effect to the sale of which we had been notified that Mr. Galinas, the secretary of the department, asked Mr. Loy, in the ordinary way of business, for a map of the town. Mr. Gelinas was not then aware of the different phases through which the sale had passed, X was not obliged to tell my Hon. Mr. TARTE.
officers what I had done. Mr. Galinas acted in the ordinary way of business. He communicated with the sitting member for information which he might have got elsewhere. Surely if there had been any desire to conceal that transaction from the public, the Deparment of Public Works would have acted differently. The whole thing was carried out in perfect good faith. My hon. friend was surprised at the delay that took place in completing the purchase. Well, in the month of August the ministers were away, I was away, and it was only on the 17th of September that I ordered a report to be prepared. There was no sitting of the Council, and some time afterwards I resigned. Therefore, the delay on which my hon. friend has laid so much stress is very easily explained. The correspondence between Mr. Gelinas and Mr. Loy is also very easily explained. I do not desire to say much more on that question; I am a layman, and am judging things of that kind in the ordinary way in which laymen judge them. Mr. Loy gave an option on the 14th of July. On the 16th of July that option was executed and a sum of money paid in cash as a guarantee of good faith. From that day Mr Loy considered himself no longer the owner of the property. Mr. Dandurand had appointed Mr. Johnston as his agent without the knowledge of Mr. Loy or the Department of Public Works. Mr. Johnston carried out his mission in concealing from Mr. Loy the object of his errand. He went to the town of Valleyfield and explained to Mr. Lov that he wanted the property for commercial purposes. Mr. Loy inquired whether the purchase was for the government, and Mr. Johnston said no it was for other purposes. Mr. Loy did not know a word about the object of Mr. Johnston's mission, he did not know Johnston. On information that he received, my hon. friend took upon himself to assert that he was in a position to prove that Johnston was acting on behalf of the sitting member and that the sitting member was trying fraudulently to evade the law. That is the charge made. It is that Mr. I.oy, knowing that he could not sell directly, appointed Mr. Johnston as his agent and that the two men were acting fraudulently. That charge my hon. friend has tried to prove. He has admitted himself that Mr. Johnston acted all through as the paid agent of Mr. Dandurand, and consequently of the government. It is evident that Johnston never acted as the agent of Mr. Loy. Then I ask: How can the sitting member be said to have been guilty of any fraudulent act? The House and the country will say no. Any man of good faith will say no. And without casting any reproach on my hon. friend, accepting his statement that lie has acted in good faith, I verily believe he would have acted more creditably to himself and have shown greater regard for

the honour and dignity of the House, if lie had agreed to the suggestion made to him by the right lion, gentleman who leads the House, and accepted the statement which Mr. Loy and myself made on our honour that the transaction had been carried out in the way it has been. But my hon. friend, proceeding on information he had received from the outside, saw fit not to accept our statement. The question was referred to the Committee on Privileges and Elections. Mr. Loy was examined under oath. He repeated under oath what he had said in the House, that he did not know for whom Mr. Johnston was buying his property. I was examined under oath, and I swore that Mr. Loy never approached me nor did I approach him since his election to parliament. It is true that in 1898, before Mr. Loy was a member, and when lie was the first magistrate of the town of Valleyfield, a petition was signed suggesting as a suitable site for a public building, Mr. Loy's property. Parliament had not then voted any money for a public building. But the citizens of the town of Valleyfield were anxious to have a public building, and they recommended the Loy property as the best site. When Mr. Loy signed that petition, he had sold his property to a Mr. Arc-hambault, and was no longer the owner. Later on, however, Archam-beault did not pay, and Mr. Loy took it back. When he signed the petition in 1898 he was not the owner, but even if he had been, he was not a member of parliament, and but only the mayor of the town; and though it might be said to be a little risky, he had right, as well as anybody else, to sign the petition. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier has reminded the House that in 1898 Mr. Loy had sold to Mr. Archambault for the sum
einnAA0,?' tljat tlle government paid 8iu,uuo tor the same property; but my hon friend knows that it is clearly established in the evidence that from 1898 to 1902 property in Valleyfield has increased by leaps and bounds. One of the statements which my hon. friend has made in his indictment is that the property sold to the government was sold at a price exceeding its value, and that the assessors had valued it at $5,000. In point of fact, the indictment of my hon. friend, from beginning to end, is a charge of fraudulent conduct between Mr. Loy and myself, because if the property had been paid far too high, if Mr. Loy acted fraudulently in bonding it to Mr. Johnston, both Mr. Loy and myself are guilty. I am guilty for having closed my eyes to a trans-aetion in which a member of parliament was involved and also to the fact that the property was purchased at too high a price. Sir, I took every possible precaution, and the evidence justifies my course from beginning to end. The evidence has established that property in Valleyfield is assessed at two-thirds and sometimes one-half of its
value. One of the assessors, himself a political friend of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, swore that in his official capacity he was accustomed to value property at two-thirds and sometimes at one-half its real value.
That point is clear, and on that score, as to the others, my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) lias failed, I know he has acted in good faith. He had his information from parties who have told him stories that he should not have believed. The transaction was carried on in an honest way ; and, indeed, I can only repeat what I said on a former occasion, that I am so sorry that my hon. friend the sitting member for Beauharnois has been subjected to such an annoyance. Let me tell the House that no more honest man has ever lived in any country than my hon. friend from Beauharnois. He is an honest man in the very best sense of the word. And that is the main reason, perhaps why the French Roman Catholic riding of Beauharnois elected him, an elder in the Presbyterian church, as their representative in this House. He was an honest man then, he is an honest man to-day. He has not violated the law willingly or knowingly, and I hope he has not violated even the letter of the law. The proverb says that the letter of the law kills. I hope' it will not kill on the present occasion, for the spirit of the law has not been violated. The hon. member for Beauharnois did not know what I was doing in this matter. I concealed my actions from him ; the department concealed their actions from him. He has acted in perfect good faith ; he has sold at its real value a property that could be sold to-day at a profit. It is in evidence that a property smaller than his could not be bought then for less than $13,000 cash. The value of property in the town of Valleyfield has ^ been going up by leaps and bounds*within recent years.
Well, Sir, I think I have covered all the points that deserve to be covered : The property was not bought too dear ; Mr. Lov had no knowledge of the object for which it was purchased ; Mr. Johnston did not act as his agent. There remains nothing except the fact that my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier has been wrongly informed by parties who had other purposes to serve than promoting the public interest. I quite understand that political warfare must be carried on. It is a case of political warfare on the part of the Informants of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier. He lias given his word to us and to the country and I take his word. But our word must be taken also. While taking my hon. friend's word, as I am glad to do. and as I am bound to do. yet I say without hesitation that those who informed him have been acting from purely party motives. Such sentiments should not be-and I hope will not often have occasion to be-ventilated in this House. When the case is as clear as

it has been made, it seems to me we should not have held the long investigation we have held, the result of which is now known to the country at large.

A's I was a member of the committee to which this question was referred, and as I concurred in the minority report now under discussion. I desire to say, in as few words as possible, why I formed the opinion I did, that the minority report should be sent to this House, and why I think this House should receive and adopt it. The question was not one as put by the non. member for St. Mary s (Hon. Mr. Tarte) of the moral wrong or moral guilt upon the part of the member for Beauharnois, but whether that gentleman committed an act, which, under the statute relating to the independence of parliament voided his seat. The question arose under section 10, which is in these words :
No person, directly or indirectly, alone or with any other, by himself or by the intei position of any trustee or third party, holding or enjoying, undertaking or executing any contract or agreement expressed or implied, with or for the government of Canada, on behalf of the Crown, or with or for any officer of the government of Canada, for which any public money of Canada is to be paid, shall he eligible as a member of the House of Commons, or shall sit or vote in the said House.
Now, the sole question was whether Mr. Loy, while member for Beauharnois, had brought himself within the terms of that section. Of one thing there is no question whatever, Mr. Speaker, that the Department of Public Works intended to buy this property from Mr. Loy. There is no question whatever that the department resolved to make that purchase through the interposition of an agent. The minister employed a Mr. Dandurand to make the purchase, and that agent of the government simply sent an employee of his to do the work. Now, what occurred ? Mr. Johnston, who was the sub-ageut or employee of Mr. Dau-durand, went down to Valleyfield and there saw Mr. Loy. After an hour's discussion, or less than an hour's discussion, Mr. Johnston obtained a written option from Mr. Loy for the purchase of this property for $10,000. Now, just here it is necessary to recall the fact that for three or four years prior to the closing of this transaction, the construction of a public building in Valleyfield and the purchase of property for that purpose was a burning question there. Before Mr. Loy became a member of the House, while he was mayor of Valleyfield, he had taken part in deputations that had come to Ottawa to urge that a public building should be constructed in Valleyfield, which was within what afterwards became his constituency. It was known to him that many of the people of Valleyfield were urging that Mr. Loy's own property should be purchased by the government for the purpose of this public building. Mr. Hon. Mr. TARTE.
Loy first became a member of this House in 1900, and at the following session there was a sum of $10,000 placed in the estimates for the purpose of this public building in Valleyfield. Under circumstances that we need not go into here, Mr. Loy lost his seat in this House, and was subsequently re-elected at a by-election. He became a member of this House again in 1902, and again the vote of $10,000 was placed in the estimates and granted by this House for the purpose of this public building. So it stood until July, 1902, when this Mr. Johnston being sent out by the agent of the government, saw Mr. Loy and negotiated with him for the purchase of the Loy property. And, shortly, they agreed that there should be an option given for two days to sell this property to Mr. Johnston in his name for the same sum of $10,000,, the amount that was in the estimates for the building at Valleyfield. Mr. Johnston, in the course of the conversation, was asked by Mr. Loy this question :
Well, Mr. Loy said, now it is not for the government is it ?
Now, Mr. Speaker, what induced Mr. Loy to ask that question ? Was it not his consciousness that what had been going on for three or four years was now culminating in the purchase of the property ? Was it not his suspicion, at least, that the person who was there offering to him, or willing to contract with him for $10,000 to buy this property, was really an undisclosed agent of the government ? He asked him a question, and what is the answer ? Mr. Johnston says :
That, Mr. Loy, is a matter that interests me, whether I wish to deal with outsiders or the government.
Now, surely that answer alone was sufficient to put Mr. Loy upon inquiry, he know- -ing at the time that he could not sell that property to the government without forfeiting his seat in parliament But the matter does not rest there. There are further circumstances that bring the knowledge more clearly to Mr. Loy. The acceptance declared that Mr. Johnston was to complete the purchase, and obtain his deed, and pay the purchase money within fifteen days. He did not do so, and apparently nothing was done. The matter was allowed to lie in suspense until December, but some correspondence passed in the meantime. On the 8th of September a clerk in the Public Works Department telegraphs to Mr. Loy :
Kindly see the city clerk and ask him to forward us by next mail, if possible, a copy of the plan of the city of Valleyfield, which is needed to complete the purchase of site for public building
Now, I would call attention to the fact that at this time the contract with Johnston was in suspense, no action was taken upon it. Mr. Loy knew that the question of the

public building related to his property ; he knew he had given an option to this man and had not yet received his purchase money, yet without a word with the department without a word of inquiry he sends the plan. ' Are you buying some property ; whose property are you buying ?- would have been natural questions for the member for the constituency to ask, especially in the interests of the citizens of Valley-field. He gets that plan, and he sends it to the Public Works Department with this letter :
Your telegram received last night. I send you herewith, inclosed, the only plan of the town which I could get. I am informed that Mr. Sullivan, the former engineer of the town, has a new plan, but he is away from home today. I will see him on his return, and if he will lend it I will send it or take it up to you. I would call your attention to the fact that at present there are two post offices in the town, one in the central part and another near the Canada Atlantic Railway station, in Bellerive ward.
These latter words ,are significant,, as' written by a gentleman who had no knowledge that his own property was being bought by the government. There Mr. Toy clearly shows that he knows what is the object of this purchase, it was in connection with a further post office that the town was claiming, and which the government was about to construct, and for which a vote was in the estimates of the year. The plan being sent, the clerk in the Public Works Department writes a further letter, which even more clearly brings home to Mr. Loy the knowledge that it was his own property that was being dealt with :
I have to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 9th September instant, inclosing a copy of the plan of the city of Valley-field, said plan being required by the department In connection with the purchase of Mr. R. B. Johnston's property.

Johnston was the man who held an option for the purchase of that property from Mr. Loy, the man who was in default, who had not carried out his undertaking to pay for the property within fifteen days. Johnston is apparently selling this property to the government, and Mr. Loy is to be assumed as supposing that he was acting as a man who had acquired and then owned the property, and was selling it again for an advance, perhaps, upon the price. Now, is it conceivable that that could be so ? Is it possible to conceive for one moment that a man of the Intelligence that we all know Mr. Loy possesses, would not see at once that Mr. Johnston was simply an intermediary of the government, and that he had been sent there to get round the provision of the statute ; Mr. Loy knew he could not sell to the government directly, that the government ought not to buy from, him directly, and so a Mr. Johnston was interposed ? Mr. Johnston gets an option to purchase, he does not carry it out, 252
but the transaction is going on in the Public Works Department, and Mr. Loy is asked to furnish a plan. He knows it is to be for a public building, and he knows it has relation to this Mr, Johnston who held an option from him, and he would have us believe that he had no suspicion that the purchase by Johnston was for the government.
Now, I do not wish to occupy any longer the time of the House. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier has gone into the whole of the circumstances very fully. I can only say, Mr. Speaker, that if, under such circumstances as are here stated, it is possible for a member of this House to sell property to the government through an intermediary, the Independence of Parliament Act is absolutely waste paper. Any member can buy from or can sell to the government, and the government can buy from any member by merely sending down a person to carry out the transaction, a third person, who is merely a nominal party in the bargain. I do not wish to comment further upon the case except to say this, that although Mr. Low was kept until the 1st of December- the option having been given in July, to be carried out within fifteen days-although he was kept until the 1st of December before he got his money, he allowed Mr. Johnston to keep $300 out of the prchase money ; instead of allowing him to keep $300 out of the purchase money, if there was anything that one side should be paid by the other, it was that Mr. Loy should have received interest from Mr. Johnstou.

I do not propose to detain the House very long ; I think it will be sufficient for me to make but a few remarks in regard to this matter. The facts as they are now before us were disclosed at the beginning of the session, all the circumstances were communicated to the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Cas-grain), but he did not think them of sufficient Importance to warrant him in taking any action upon them. We are told by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) that he knew of these facts previously to the beginning of the session. He has told us that he ,1s very anxious to preserve the rules and privileges of the House ; and yet he sat in his seat and allowed Mr. Loy to sit here for four months and a half in violation, as he believed, of the statute, without saying one word. He did not move in the matter until he was urged to do so by some influence or other, and that influence cannot have been from the hon. gentlemen who sit upon the other side of the House, because they did not take enough interest in the matter to appear before the committee, only two or three of them. I do not know where the influence came from, but I have a very shrewd suspicion. Now, the facts that were disclosed to us are these : First, that Mr. Loy, in January, 1898, gave a promise of sale of this piece of property to Mr. Archambau'lt, and that



that promise of sale was afterwards discharged, along in June. So far, there is no dispute. But there was the further statement in the charge that, although this promise was absolute, there was a secret agreement between Mr. Loy and Mr. Archarn-bault which raised a suspicion that the promise was given for the purpose of enabling Mr. Archambault to make a sale of the property to the government in the interest [DOT] of Mr. Loy. Mr. Archambault came upon the stand and testified himself, strongly, that such was not the case, that 'there was no agreement whatever between himself and Mr. Loy to that effect, and Mr. Loy said the same thing. It further transpired that Mr. Archambault took possession of the property. During the months that he had it he moved the buildings and did other things and made a loss of $800, and he only failed to carry out the arrangement because he could not get the money for that purpose. The committee very properly concluded that this transaction in 1898 had nothing whatever to do with what has been charged against Mr. Loy. Another matter that has been charged against Mr. Loy is that the purchase by the government of this property was a purchase by the government from Mr. Loy through the agency of Mr. Johnston. The words of the charge are as follows :
That from the time the said George Loy handed his said property to Archambault up to the day of the sale of said property to the Crown or government of Canada, he never ceased to be the proprietor of said property, and that at the time of the sale of said property on the 20th January, 1903, said Robert Bruce Johnston was merely acting for and on behalf of said Loy, who in said manner did indirectly sell his said property to the Crown or government of Canada, in violation of chapter II. of the Revised Statutes of Oanada, ' An Act respecting the Senate and House of Commons."
I will admit that if the statement had bee") correct, then Mr. Loy would have violated the statute, but it is not correct eveu according to the statement of the hon. member (Mr. Monk) himself, because, to-day, upon the floor of this House, he does not pretend to say that Mr. Johnston was the agent of Mr. Loy, hut he turns it now and says that Mr. Johnston was the agent of the government. There is the crux of the whole situation. If he had been the agent of Mr. Loy, or if he had to the knowledge of Mr. Loy been the agent of the government, then, there would have been a violation of the statute, but surely no hon. member would pretend to say that if Mr. Johnston was not the agent of Mr. Loy, and if Mr. Loy had no knowledge of the agency of Mr. Johnston on behalf of the government, Mr. Loy has committed any breach of the statute. If I am not correct in that, then, I will warn hon. gentlemen on the other side to be very *careful before they sell property, because the government could sand out an agent to purchase a piece of property no matter how Mr. WADE (Annapolis).
small from one of their number and then some hon. member might get up in the House make a charge against the party selling the property and we would have to turn him out. That is a proposition that the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker), a lawyer stands up in the House and makes. It seems a surprising thing that he should pretend to support such a proposition as that. Let us refer to the statute and see what it says. Section 10, I believe, is the section that hon. gentlemen opposite claim has been violated :
No person, directly or indirectly, alone or with any other, by himself or by the interposition of any trustee or third party, holding or enjoying, undertaking or executing, any contract or agreement, expressed or implied, with or for the government of Canada on behalf of the Crown, or with or for any of the officers of the government of Canada, for which any public money of Canada is to be paid, shall be eligible as a member of the House of Commons, or shall sit or vote in the said House.
I would like hon. gentlemen to note well the construction of this section :
No person, directly or indirectly, alone or with any other, by himself or by the interposition of any trustee or third party, &c.
That is if he sells the property to the government himself he commits an offence. If he sells the property by means of an agent or trustee then he violates the statute. That is the reasonable construction of the statute, and that is the evil that the statute was intended to remedy. The object of the statute was to put it beyond the power of the government to in any indirect way bribe the representatives who sit in the House, hut I cannot conceive of any lawyer pretending to argue in favour of the other interpretation.

If an agent of the government goes to a member of parliament and buys a property from him and the member of parliament does not know at that time that the agent is the agent of the government but he discovers it before the bargain is completed that this man is really buying for the government does the hon. gentleman think that is not covered by the statute ?
I did not say that at all.
I want to know.

The hon. gentleman shall know. I thought I made the hon. gentleman understand me as I went along, but, if I have failed, that is my misfortune. If he finds out before the sale is completed of course he does know. My proposition is simply this, and it is so plain to my mind that it does not need any demonstration, that if the party does not know at all surely he cannot be liable under this section, but if be does know that the agent is acting for the government, then, of course, he is liable.
Hear, hear.

My bon. friends say ' bear, bear.' I am glad tliat I have been able to make them see this thing as I see it. The question is :	Did Mr. Loy know that Mr. Johnston was acting as agent for the government ? I make bold to say that there is not one word of testimony to support that position. But, there is the emphatic evidence of Mr. Boy, the emphatic evidence of Mr. Tarte, and the emphatic evidence of Mr. Johnston, all the other way showing that Mr. Loy did not know that Mr. Johnston was acting as the agent of the government. What did Mr. Loy know, and what did Mr. Johnston say ? Mr. Loy, in the first instance, asked Mr. Johnston if this property was for the government. It was a very ordinary question to ask. What answer did he receive ? It is a question for me whether I deal with the government or with outsiders. That was Mr. Johnston's reply. Is that not a proper answer for a man who is buying property to make ? If I go to Mr. A to buy his property from him, if he states his price and I am willing to give the price, has Mr. A any right to limit the parties to whom I shall sell that property ? If Mr. Johnston had bona fide purchased the property had he not a perfect right to go out and sell it to the government the next day or at any time that he saw fit ? Mr. Johnston gave Mr. Loy to understand that he needed the property for a departmental store, and Mr. Loy has told us in his testimony that he believed that he was selling the property to him, but I submit here as a reasonable proposition that if Mr. Loy, at the time he sold his property, believed honestly in his mind that he was selling it to Mr. Johnston it does not make the slightest difference what was in the mind of Mr. Johnston. When did Mr. Loy have the first knowledge that the government was going to get this property ? According to his evidence it was long afterwards, nearly two months afterwards on the receipt from the secretary of the Department of Public Works of the letter acknowledging the receipt of a plan he had sent and which letter stated that the plan was required for the purpose of concluding the purchase of the property from Mr. Johnston.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

I hope my hon. friends will be quiet until I am done. At that time had Mr. Loy knowledge that Mr. Johnston had negotiated a sale of the property to the government ? Certainly, and he does not deny that for a moment, but he had no knowledge at the time Mr. Johnston was acting as agent of the government in the purchase of the property.

I was not able to be at the committee all the time and the evidence not having been printed. I am obliged to ask questions to know what the evidence was, because I have no means of knowing.
252i
Did Mr. Loy say where he supposed the government were going to build the post office ?

I do not know that there was ever anything said about it. There was an attempt on the part of Mr. Monk to prove that the government had a site there which they could have built on, but he has abandoned that as he has abandoned the statement made by him that the price paid for this property was too large. The statement made by Mr. Loy was that he had no knowledge of the government getting this property until long after he had concluded the terms of sale, and had received $100 on account.
And did not get the consideration.

Certainly he did not get the consideration; that has been stated half a dozen times over. He only received $100 on account, and he was under promise to convey the property to Mr. Johnston, and the evidence shows that he did not know that Johnston was the agent of the government until long after the deed had been passed and until after the whole money had been paid to him. I am not quite as suspicious as some hon. gentlemen opposite and that is the reason why I am not ready to condemn any man upon the mere statement of so flimsy a suspicion as has been put forward here. The last speaker also tried to make the point, that the option of sale was given in July for fifteen days, and that the sale was not concluded until December. Why, to my mind, that and the explanations that were given, afford the strongest argument in favour of the honesty of Mr. Loy and of his innocence and want of knowledge in this whole matter. The negotiations were going on and this Mr. Johnston was trying to get the money. It was a continuous contract, it had never been ended by Mr. Loy, he was anxious to sell his property, he needed the money to clear off the mortgage upon it, and finally at the suggestion of Johnston Who said he had trouble in raising the money and that Loy would have to drop $300 from the price in order to enable him to expedite the obtaining of the money, Loy did so, and then Johnston went and negotiated his note with the Sovereign Bank in Montreal, obtained the money and paid it into the hands of the notary who, with the proceeds discharged the mortgage that was on the property and handed over the balance to Mr. Loy. Now it does seem to me that the only question we had to consider, and the only question we have to consider to-day is :	Whether the statement of Mr. Loy in that connection is true or false. He has undertaken to swear, and he is supported in it by three other witnesses. that he never knew that Johnston was an agent of the government until after the deed had been passed. That is exactly the evidence and it is just as it appears.

He did know on September 16th that the government was buying property from Johnston and that is the statement contained in the letter-
' The hon. gentleman has made a very important statement, and might I ask him when was the deed passed V
The deed was signed in December if my memory serves me.
Then surely he had the knowledge on the 8th September according to your own admission.

Not at all. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) does not seem to follow my remarks for the purpose of getting information, or otherwise he would have heard what I stated, and I stated it as emphatically as I could : that on the 16th day of September by the letter which Mr. Loy received from the secretary of the department, it was conveyed to his mind that the government was buying this property from Mr. Johnston. That is what X stated.
Yes.
Now, I say that if Mr. Johnston purchased the property bona fide from Mr. Loy, had he not a perfect right to turn around and sell it to the government V

We have not the evidence before us owing to the action that the government has taken, and so we do not understand this matter thoroughly, and consequently I have to ask a question. When was the sale from Loy to Johnston completed V
The sale from Loy to Johnston was completed, if my memory serves me right on the first or second day of December.
I thought that was the date of the sale from Johnston to the Crown.
No. The date of the sale from Johnston to the government was away along in January.
Is it a fact that this letter came to Mr. Loy's possession some six weeks before he completed the sale to Mr. Johnston V
That is perfectly right. It came to his possession on or about the 16th or 17th of September.
The 8th of September.

The 8th of September, perhaps; it does not matter for a few days. That letter conveyed to his mind exactly what I have stated, that Johnston and the government were negotiating the purchase of that property.

I shall have to ask the hon. gentleman another question.
' Mr, WADE.
We have to get at the facts in this fragmentary way, not having the evidence printed. I do not quite understand the explanation of the rebate of $300 on the price. It has been alleged that the payment of $300 was really a commission paid by Mr. Loy to Mr. Johnston for his services as agent. My hon. friend (Mr. Wade) conveys a different view Which must of course be considered because I was impressed by the statement made from this side of the House. My hon. friend (Mr. Wade) says that was an abatement and not a commission paid to Mr. Johnston; it was an abatement of the price which Mr. Johnston had agreed in the first instance to pay to Mr. Loy. Will my hon. friend give us the evidence as fully as possible with regard to that, because I think it bears pretty strongly upon the point we have to decide.

The evidence upon this point is : That the purchase price agreed upon between Loy and Johnston was $10,000, and there was to be no commission paid by Mr. Loy to Mr. Johnston and there was never any talk about commission at all.
Naturally there would not be-if it was a mere purchase.

It was a mere purchase. That was at the beginning of the transaction. Time went on until about the first of December or the last of November, when Mr. Johnston comes to Mr. Loy and tells him that he has great difficulty in securing the money and that Mr. Loy will have to make a reduction in the price-that is the evidence-and Mr. Loy who was in need of the money at the time finally agreed to make a reduction of $300 in the price.
May I ask my hon. friend another question ? I have to apologize to him for interrupting him, but it is because of the evidence not being printed.
I am glad to have the hon. gentleman do so.
Did Mr. Loy, at that time, inquire of Mr. Johnston what he was getting from the government ?

When on the first or second of December an agreement was made to change the price, would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wade) who is a prominent lawyer, inform the House whether he would regard that as a new contract entered into at that time, Mr. Johnston being in default on the first agreement ?

Certainly not. I would simply regard it as a modification of one of the terms of the contract that existed between them. There is no question about that. I do not know that I have anything more to say about this matter, Mr. Speaker.
I should, I suppose, express my regret that my conduct as chairman of the committee was not pleasing to the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, but then you know there is a certain class of lawyers who are very much given to abusing the judge who decides against them in a suit they should never have brought, and I do not see why 1 should not allow that privilege to my hon. friend (Mr. Monk).

Let me give my view of this transaction in just a few words.
I will deal with the minority report and from that report it seems to me that there was an option got by a man named Johnston, who was agent for Mr. Dandurand in Montreal, who was employed by the Minister of Public Works for the purpose of purchasing this property. That option was obtained in July. The termination of the option was on the 31st of July. For that option he paid -Si 00, Mr. Loy covenanting that he would have the right to purchase the property for $10,000. On the 8th of September, long after the option had expired, there is a letter or a telegram from an officer of the Department of Public Works, asking Mr. Loy to send up plans of this particular property.
Some hon. MEMEBRS. No, no.

I will read the telegram :
I have to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 9th September, inst., inclosing a copy of the plan of the city of Valleyfield, said plan being required by the department in connection with the purchase of Mr. R. B. Johnston's property.
For what purpose was the plan required 1 For the purpose of the purchase of the property. The hon. chairman of the committee admits that Mr. Loy must have had knowledge that the government were purchasing this property when he received this letter. Then Mr. Loy had knowledge on the 8th of September that his property was being purchased by the government for the purpose of a public building. He was theta! under no obligation whatever to convey that property to Mr. Johnston.
Why not ?
The option had expired on the 31st of July.
That is not the fact.
Then I am misinformed from the documents. The option was on the 16th of July, and was for fifteen days.
No, no.

Read the option and its acceptance. Is it an option for ever? When does it expire ? The option expires within the fifteen days mentioned, and Mr. Loy was not obliged at any time afterwards to convey the property. At any rate, on the 8th of September following, he had notice from the government that the purchase was made on behalf of the government, and he makes a conveyance of the property on the 1st of December following, receiving the money and giving the deed. Is not that a knowledge by the party who is selling the property that he is virtually conveying it to the government which had purchased it for the purpose of erecting a post office ?

I will not go over the ground convened by the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade), but I want to state how this matter strikes me. What are the facts in this case ? On the 14th of July, Mr. Johnston, who was acting as the agent of Mr. Dandurand in acquiring this property-and I am prepared to admit at once that the latter was the agent of the Department of Public Works-obtained an option from Mr. Loy which was to be exercised on the 16th of the same month. On the 16th of July the option was exercised, and $100 were paid by Mr. Johnston to Mr. Loy. There is absolutely nothing in the evidence which shows that Mr. Johnston himself knew that he was acting for the Grown. He was told by Mr. Dandurand to go and acquire this property, without being told for whom it was wanted. Mr. Dandurand himself knew that the property was required by the Crown.
Mr. Dandurand, in his evidence, makes it clear that he told Johnston that the property was required by the government.
That is not my recollection. My recollection is that Johnston himself did not know at all that the property was required by the Crown.
He did not.
And he assumed that it was required for the purpose of putting up a theatre or a departmental store.
Mr. Dandurand corrects that.
Both Dandurand and Johnston swore that Johnston did not know for whom he was purchasing.

Does not the hon. gentleman remember that when Johnston was

giving his evidence, he said that he did know that the property was required for a post office, and that he knew that when he went down to Valleyfleid ?
No.
And thought he had the right to exercise his own judgment in the selection of a site ?

I have already stated my recollection of the evidence, and there is no use my repeating it. There is at any rate no dispute about the option having been exercised on the 16th of July, when $100 were paid by Mr. Johnston to Mr. Loy. That made the position the same as if on that day, instead of an agreement to sell being made, a conveyance had been actually executed.

Is my hon. friend aware that where property, to which a trust is attached, is sold to some one who is ignorant of the trust, but who, before tbie consideration money is paid, has knowledge of the trust, he is bound by the trust?
I do not see what this has to do with the question.

Will my hon. friend permit me to tell him ? If a member of parliament was approached for the purchase of a piece of property and entered into a bargain to sell it, not knowing that it was wanted for the Crown and if, before the consideration money is paid, hie becomes aware of that fact, he would be within the terms of the statute.
I take issue with my hon. friend on that point.
The hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) was not bold enough for that.

As a lawyer, with some knowledge of the law of Quebec, where the transaction took place, such would not be the case. Let me quote an authority. My bon. friiend the leader of the opposition is perhaps not as familiar as we are with the Quebec Civil Code, but if he will turn up articles 1472 and 1476 he will find that I am right. 1472 says :
Sale is a contract by which one party gives a thing to the other for a price in money which the latter obliges himself to pay for it.
It is perfected by the consent alone of the parties although the thing sold is not then delivered.
Consent makes the sale perfect, and my contention is that on the 16th of July the title of the property passed from Loy to Johnston, and that anything that happened subsequently did not change the legal position of the parties. Article 1476 says :
A simple promise of a sale is not equivalent to a sale, but the creditor may demand that the debtor shall execute a deed of sale in his favour

according to the terms of the promise, and, in default of so doing, that the judgment shall be equivalent to such deed and have all its legal effects ; or he may recover damages according to the rules contained in the title of obligations.
On the 17th of July, and from that day until the 20th of January, 1903, when this conveyance was made, Mr. Johnston had the right to say to Mr. Loy : ' You must convey that property to me.' And if Mr. Loy had refused Mr. Johnston could have enforced his claim in the courts.

Does the hon. gentleman say that the decisions I have quoted, and which have been uniformly followed in the province of Quebec, namely, that if a man does not conform to the conditions stated in the option, he cannot claim the property ?
That is jurisprudence, not law.
In my opinion, a promise of sale, under the circumstances disclosed, accompanied by a payment on account, is as good a title as a conveyance. Does my hon. friend dispute that as a sound proposition ?
Of course I will deny that. I have quoted authority to show that you must conform to the conditions of the option.

That is not a denial of my proposition. I am sure the hon. gentleman would be very careful about denying the proposition of law I have put. If that be so, the knowledge which Mr. Loy acquired some time in September-and I admit for the sake of argument that he received notice that the Department of Public Works wanted his property for this public building
He received notice that they had bought it.

Assuming that Mr. Loy knew beyond doubt that that property was required for public purposes, he could not avoid the transaction which he had concluded with Mr. Johnston on the 16th July without laying himself open to an action at law to compel him to execute that conveyance. In order to determine whether this transaction was a violation of the Independence of Parliament Act, wie must go back to the 16th of July ; and if on that day the transaction was perfectly legitimate, then Mr. Loy did not commit any violation of the Act. There is absolutely nothing in the evidence which would warrant any one believing that Mr. Loy on the 16th of July had been notified or knew that the property was required by Johnston for other purposes than a departmental stone or theatre. But hon. gentlemen opposite argue that the option had lapsed and that, as a matter of law, Mr. Loy could have

avoided the agreement he made on the 16th of July and should have avoided it because of the knowledge he had since acquired.
I submit that that is also wrong in law. Under the law of the province of Quebec, he was bound to carry out bis agreement. The delay in executing a deed of conveyance only gave him the right to claim interest. Article 1077 says :
The damages resulting from the delay in the payment of money, to which the debtor is liable, consist only of the interest at the rate legally agreed upon by the parties, or, in the absence of such agreement, at the rate fixed by law.	.
So far as the law is concerned, Mr. Loy was bound to carry it out notwithstanding the knowledge he had acquired two months later on. I want to point out a very glaring contradiction on the part of my kon. friend from Jacques Cartier, which shows most conclusively that-in his own mind, although perhaps he did not realize it for the moment-he was satisfied that the charge against Mr. Loy is disproved. Look at paragraph 8:
That from the time the said George Loy handed his said property to Archambault up to the day of the sale of the said property to the Crown or government of Canada, he never ceased to be the proprietor of said property-and that at the time of the sale of said property on the 20th January, 1903

*-
-and I call the attention of hon. members of the House to the following words :
-^said Robert Bruce Johnston was merely acting for and on behalf of the said Loy.
So, my hon. friend charges that Mr. Johnston was the agent of Mr. Loy. And that was the charge, I submit that my hon. friend must prove in order to establish the fact that there had been a violation of the statutes.

Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Belcourt) permit me to ask him a question ? What would be the effect of the fifteen days mentioned in the acceptance of that option according to the laws of the province of Quebec ? How, long, for instance, after that fifteen days had expired would Johnston have the right to enforce that contract ? Will it go on for ever ?
No, it does not go on for ever. The delay of fifteen days, as I understand it, was required by Johnston himself within which
For looking into titles

Yes-within which Loy should convey the property to him. But there were difficulties in the way. Johnston was quite satisfied to take his deed later on. and I say that is all that we must look to, because Loy was hound to do that which Johnston required of him, notwithstanding the lapse of fifteen days.
Then, he could enforce it five years hence ?

I cannot make my point if I am interrupted in this way. I was going to say that my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier made the charge that Johnston was the agent of Loy ; and I say, and I think he will agree with me, that, in order to claim that Loy has committed a violation of the section, it was necessary to establish that point. For the section-section 10-says :
No person, directly o.r indirectly, alone or with any other, by himself or by the Interposition of any trustee or any third party, holding or enjoying, undertaking or executing any contract or agreement expressed or implied, with or for the government of Canada on behalf of the Crown, or with or for any officers of the government of Canada for which any public money of Canada is to be paid, shall be eligible as a member of the House of Commons or shall sit or vote in the said House.
What the Act contemplates is an agent on the part of the member against whom the charge is made, and not an agent on the part of the Crown. Otherwise, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) the seat of every member of this House would be in jeopardy continually. The statute provides that a member of the House shall not directly by himself or through am agent endeavour to sell his property to the Crown. And now, what has the hon. member for Jacques Cartier asked this House to declare ? Jtfot only in his argument has he stated that it is not proven that Johnston was the agent of Loy, but by reference to the report which his* motion asks this House to adopt, we find these words :
Under these circumstances, Mr. Loy could not have remained ignorant of the fact that Johnston, in the transaction with Mr. Loy, was an agent of the government.
Remember, Mr. Speaker, that the charge was that Johnston was the agent of Loy. Yet, my hon. friend is asking us to-day to declare* that Johnston was the agent of the government. There is a flat contradiction which, to my mind, shows conclusively that the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, in dealing with this evidence, himself concluded that the charge he had brought that Johnston was the agent of Loy had been disproved. Nobody disputes that Johnston was the agent of the government-he was employed by Mr. Dandurand, who, was the agent of the Crown. But Mr. Loy did not know this. And surely we are not going to declare that a member of this House has violated the independence of parliament by the sale of property if, on that day, he did not know that the purchaser was the agent of the Crown. The hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) would not follow the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). He does not ask this House to say that there was any actual moral-X think he called it-violation of the statute, as the hon. member for Jacques Cartier tells us.

The hon. member (Mr. Belcourt) must allow me to explain that I did not say that. I stated that it was not a question of moral wrong, but simply a question of whether there had, been a violation of the words of the statute.
I understood my hon. friend (Mr. Barker) to say that the most he would contend for was that there was a technical violation of the statute.
No.

Then, I do not press that. But it is clear that the hon. member for Jacques Cartier has been compelled to say in this minority report that the other two charges that he made, namely, that the price was excessive, and that there was other property in Valleyfield suitable and available for the purpose of a public building, were disproved.

My hon. friend (Mr. Belcourt) must not misrepresent the report. It is said in the minority report, that we have confined the report to the direct question submitted to the committee. My hon. friend remembers perfectly well the nature of the evidence as to the value of the property as well as its availability as a site.

I take it that if the hon. member (Mr. Monk) had been able to show to his- own satisfaction that the price was excessive, he would not have been content to let that go without calling attention to it. Had it been shown by the evidence that the price paid by the ex-Minister of Public Works was excessive, it would have been the hon. member's duty to say so. Why did he include this in his charge if it was not relevant and necessary ? I think that the hon. member failed, on his own admission to show that too much was' paid for the site or that there were other sites in the town available. And as to the other charge, the hon. member disposes of that himself by this motion declaring that Johnston was the agent for the government. The very essence of his charge was that Johnston was the agent of Mr. Loy. To establish that charge it must be shown that Loy must have known, at the time when the property was being acquired, that it was being acquired for the government. It seems to me that after the statement made by the hon. member for Beauharnois and the statement made by the hon. member for St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) might well have withdrawn his charge, because the evidence he had before him in the documents-and there is a great deal of documentary evidence-goes to show that, until two months after this option was given. Mr. Loy could never have known that this property was being acquired for government purposes. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier tells us, and we are bound to take his word for it, that he

7
has no ulterior motives in making the charge. But, while we here are bound to accept his word, I think people outside will have a very shrewd idea that this was an attempt, perhaps on the part of a gentleman who used to sit in this House, if not on the part of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, to avenge himself upon a political opponent. I submit that the charges that were brought have been disproved by the evidence. And, in order to justify the vote I intend to give, I want nothing better than my hon. friend's own statement, contained in his motion, that Johnston was the agent of the government, and not the a'gent of Mr. Loy.

I did not intend to make any remarks on this matter, but the very astounding propositions laid down by my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt) compel me to say a word or two. In the first place, I think it most unfortunate that the right hon. leader of the House, who, next to the Speaker, is responsible for the dignity and decorum of this House, saw fit, in his wisdom, to insist that we should discuss this matter without having the evidence printed and before us. The motion which the right hon. gentleman saw fill to have passed yesterday was that this question of the printing should be referred, if you please, to a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons. That is the position the matter stands in to-day. This question of printing the evidence touching the honour, and privileges, and prerogatives of this House is to be referred to a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons to determine whether it shall be printed. I do not regard that as a proper way of dealing with the question, and I venture to think that it was most unfortunate that the right hon. gentleman did not see fit to assent to the motion of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier to have this evidence printed. We have had to-day disputes across the floor of this House about many questions of fact contained in this evidence, although we were assured yesterday that there was no possible question about any matter of fact involved in this case. The members of this House at the present time are in doubt, I am in doubt myself, as to the evidence with regard to many matters that have been mentioned.
But I wish to refer to some remarks of my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt) with regard to the effect of this statute.
I wish to speak so far as the law of my own province is concerned. I do not profess to speak with any authority with regard to that of Quebec. But so far as the law' of my own province is concerned, I beg to dissent most emphatically from the views which that hon. gentleman has laid down. The law of Nova Scotia, following in that regard the law of England, is very much the same as that which the hon. gentleman has propounded as the law of Quebec. If a con-

tract is made for the sale of land, although no deed passes at the time, although no money is paid at the time, the land in equity though not at law, becomes the property of the purchaser; the right to compensation is the right of the man who sells the land. That is the rule in equity, and that is very much like the law propounded by thp hon. gentleman as that of the province of Quebec. But I would point out to him that according to the English law-I am speaking only with regard to the English law and the law of my own province
In regard to the point at issue, as to whether delay in the payment of the purchase money would split up the whole contract and leave both parties free, what would my hon. friend say to that V
I shall come to that very fully before I sit down.
I was afraid my hon. friend would neglect that view.

I say that so far as that matter is concerned, distinctions are drawn in the English law between the position of a man who has made a formal conveyance and received the compensation money, and the position of a man who has made a contract for the land, but has not yet received a legal title and has not yet received compensation. One distinction was that to which I adverted a moment ago. Another distinction I think would be made in a case of this kind, which involves a matter of public policy, because what would follow the hon. gentleman's proposition ? Has he thought of it ? His proposition is this, that if any member of this House were approached by some person and gave that person an option of purchase which was after accepted ; then if the member discovers before the contract is completed that the other party was really the agent of and was purchasing for the government, the member can complete the contract.
I do not dispute that, but that is not the case here.

But he did dispute it a moment ago. He told us that he most solemnly affirmed upon his standing as a lawyer in this House that that man could go on and carry out that contract. My hon. friend has changed his opinion, I am glad he has changed his opinion, because I say such a doctrine as that would be a monstrous one. What would follow from it V According to the law of Nova Scotia, according to the law of England, and I suppose according to the law of Quebec, an undisclosed principal can be sued by the man with whom he has made a contract, and that being the case, as soon as a member of parliament found out that he was dealing with the government, if the government did not see tit to carry out the contract under the new conditions, you would have
the spectacle of a member of parliament bringing suit in the Exchequer Court against the government for the unpaid price of property which he had sold to the government.
I was not dealing with such a case at all, I was dealing with a different case. The case the hon. gentleman supposes is not the case here.

I am glad to see that I misunderstood my hon. friend. I would not have got up except to make an observation on what I thought he distinctly stated to this House, in answer to a question I put to him, namely that such was his view of the law of the province of Quebec.

Would the hon. gentleman allow me to) put a question to him ? When did Mr. Loy ascertain that he was selling the property to the government V I submit for his consideration that Mr. Loy never found that out until after the deed had passed, he never found that this man was acting as agent for the government.

My hon. friend's view of the case is of course entitled to all possible respect, I am not finding any fault with that. But there are circumstances in connection with this case which, in my opinion, might point to an opposite conclusion. It appears so far as I can gather from the evidence, which I have not had an opportunity of reading, that there was considerable discussion as to the probability of the property being required as a site for a post office. It appears that Mr. Johnston came to Mr. Loy and Mr. Loy was suspicious at the' time that the property might be required by the government. An option was given, which I will not refer to again, as it has been read two or three times to the House. The terms of that option were not carried out. And six weeks before Mr. Loy gave any formal conveyance of the property at all, he receives a letter from the Public Works Department, a letter of the 18th of September, in which ihe is distinctly told that certain information which is required from him with regard to a plan of the city of Yalleyfield, is required by the department in connection with the purchase of R. B. Johnston's property. Now, my hon. friend from Annapolis, or some hon. gentleman on the other side, has very ingeniously put forward this view of the situation :	They say that that merely
means that Mr. Loy, had agreed to sell to Mr. Johnston, and Mr. Johnston buying in his own right, had afterwards agreed to sell to the government. Well, that may be so, but it is rather unusual that Mr. Johnston should immediately sell to the government long before he got a title from Mr. Loy.
Not immediately, two months afterwards.

Let us say two months afterwards; and I think it is most

unfortunate for Mr. Loy ttmt lie was not called before the committee to give evidence as to bis understanding of that letter. Was be asked with regard to bis understanding of that letter ?
He was before the committee.

I know be was, but I understand he was not before the committee after this letter was produced. Am I right or wrong ? Again my bon. friend will see that I am embarrassed by the fact that, owing to the action of the government yesterday, we have not this evidence before us. Am I right or wrong in supposing that Mr. Boy did not give evidence before the committee after this letter was produced V
He did not.

Then I consider it is a very unfortunate thing that he was not called before the committee to give evidence, and to make plain to the committee what his understanding was of the purport of that letter.
He was there, why did not the hon. gentleman opposite cross question him V

I am speaking of this matter on behalf of Mr. Boy himself, because here is a letter of the 8th of September written to Mr. Loy and received by him some six weeks before this transaction was completed, and in which it is made perfectly apparent to him that the man who has come to him to get an option on his property is really proposing to convey that property to the government. Now, under these circumstances, it does seem to me very unfortunate that Mr. Loy did not again come before the committee and throw what light he could as to the condition of his mind after he had received that letter.

Assuming that Mr. Loy could have had no doubt on that day, the 8th of September, that the property acquired by Mr. Johnston was being made over to the crown, will the hon. gentleman contend that because of that knowledge on the part of Mr. Loy he would have been relieved in law from performing his contract made with Mr. Johnston on the 16th of July V
I do not know what the hon. gentleman means.
Could he have successfully resisted an action for the specific performance of the agreement of the 16th July ?
If Mr. Loy had notice, and if Mr. Loy knew that Mr. Johnston was really acting for the government-
I assume that.
I asked the hon. gentleman that once and he gave me one answer, and I ask him again and he gives me another answer.

Surely my hon. friend wants to be fair. Assuming that on the 8th September Mr. Loy acquired knowledge that tire property was being acquired by the department, could then Mr. Loy have successfully resisted an action at law on the part of Mr. Johnston for a specific performance of the agreement of the 16th July? I say no, and I would like to have my hon. friend's opinion.

If, as a matter of fact, there was, in the first instance a distinct bargain between Mr. Johnston and Mr. Loy, according to Mr. Loy's belief and that bargain had been carried out between Mr. Loy and Mr. Johnston so as to vest the title in the property to him, it would be perfectly plain that any transaction between Mr. Johnston and the government afterwards would be of no effect.
That is the whole point.
That is the whole point ?
Yes.

Well, I have very great difficulty in making myself plain to my hon. friend.
