made a bargain with your agent although I did not know he was your agent, to sell this property. I have now discovered that he was only your agent, you are now declining to carry out your bargain, and 1 come into the Exchequer Court with my petition of right, and claim from you $10,000 which was agreed to be paid for my property. Surely the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Beleourt) or any other hon. member on the other side of the House will not pretend for a moment that any such action as that would be entertained by the Exchequer Court.

Would the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him a question ? A layman may perhaps be able to make thing's clear. On the 16th September the

secretary of the Department of Public Works writes to Mr. Loy and he tells him that the department wants a map in connection with the purchase of Mr. Johnston's property. Mr. Loy considered then that he had sold his property to Mr. Johnston. Was he not simply informed that Mr. Johnston had sold to the department ? That is the point I would like to make clear.

Here is one of the difficulties In connection with which I stated a moment ago that I regarded it as most unfortunate that Mr. Loy was not called before the committee to give evidence after this letter had been produced. Do I make myself clear to my hon. friend ?
I see.

I say that the letter might possibly have the construction which the hon. gentleman puts upon it, namely that Mr. Loy might merely infer from it that Mr. Johnston had bought this property in good faith from Mr. Loy, had afterwards entered into an agreement with the Crown to convey it to the Crown, and that the Crown were therefore investigating the title and wanted a plan for that purpose. That would make Mr. Loy perfectly innocent, but if, on the other hand, this letter gave to Mr. Loy the notice that I have described a moment ago, that Mr. Johnston was not really buying the property in his own right, but buying it for the Crown, and that the Crown was taking steps for the fulfilment of the contract, an entirely different condition of affairs would exist.
It is in evidence that when Mr. Johnston went to Mr. Loy, Mr. Loy did not know that Mr. Johnston was acting for the department. He made that clear in his evidence.

Assuming that Mr. Johnston was the agent of the government, and the government the undisclosed principal, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) will admit, will he not, that Mr. Johnston could not commence action for specific performance against Mr. Loy if Mr. Loy had refused to convey to him, and if Mr. Johnston could commence action against Mr. Loy for specific performance and if Mr. Loy was innocent at the time that he made the promise to sell to Mr. Johnston, could this statute be any defence in an action for specific performance ?

It would be exactly the same defence that would arise in the action I have suggested. Does the hon. gentleman think that Mr. Loy could maintain an action against the government in the Exchequer Court ? I would hardly suppose that he would go as far as that, but if he did go as far as that, with every possible deference to the hon. gentleman's opinion, I would hardly feel justified in agreeing with him upon that point.
If the most brilliant lawyers in this House do not understand this question, what could you expect from poor Loy ?

I think that is a question which might properly be addressed to the right hon. leader of the House (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) particularly in view of the fact that he has not even permitted these lawyers to whom my hon. friend (Mr. Heyd) refers in such complimentary terms, to have an opportunity of perusing the evidence.
I am afraid it would be worse and worse if the evidence were printed.
I do not know about that.
My hon. friend can console himself with the knowledge that there was no argument before the committee at all.

I almost feel inclined to address the House now in the language of Samuel Weller before leaving the witness stand : Is there any other hon. gentleman who desires to ask me a question ? In conclusion, I have simply to say that my view of the statute is entirely different from that which has been presented by some hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. If we are to conclude from this evidence, which is not actually before us, because we have not had it printed, and from this correspondence, that Mr. Loy at all times up to the time he gave the title and received the compensation money believed that he was making a real sale of the property to Mr. Johnston, then that is one aspect of the case, and, adopting that view, we would have to acquit him ; but if, on the other hand, the evidence, the correspondence and the circumstances of the case would lead us to the conclusion that at any time up to the conveyance by him of this property and the receipt of the compensation money he became aware of the fact that Mr. Johnston was really the agent of the Crown, then it seems to me that this is not a case in which he can be justified in the way in which the majority report of the committee does seek to justify him.

Mr. Speaker, it seems almost a pity to interrupt the flow of* legal eloquence, but it is also a pity that the whole of the afternoon should be taken up without a layman expressing an opinion. I can only form an opinion from the speeches I have heard ; and, taking the defence of Mr. Loy, I can only conclude that Mr. Loy is one of the most innocent men I ever have heard of. He is too innocent to sit in this House. I dare say you all remember reading of that charming old humbug Samuel Pepys, who used to humbug himself and others, and who,

on one occasion, was controller of the King's navy, and had reason to suppose that a certain gentleman was going to offer ihim something for an appointment. This gentleman asked him to dinner, and on leaving, Mr. Pepys, in his quaint language, says : This man did hand me an envelope which, by its feel, I felt contained money ; when I got home I did open the envelope behind my back, so that if asked in future I could truly say that when I opened the envelope I saw no money there. Now, Sir, it strikes me that this simple and ordinary transaction of the purchase of a piece of property in Yalleyfleld for a post office, the negotiations for which had been going on for some years, has been so complicated and so surrounded with agents and with extraordinary conditions, that I would say it would be impossible that Mr. Loy should not have known that the government were purchasing this property. With regard to the abatement of |300 of the price, that abatement was paid, if I understood the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wade) aright, after Mr. Loy had knowledge or suspicion that the government were purchasing. That seems to me of itself a most extraordinary transaction. As the case has been presented, from a layman's point of view it would be concluded that Mr. Loy had knowledge that that property was purchased for a post office. If he had not, he is too innocent a man to represent any constituency in this House.
Mr. 0. B. HEYD (South Brant). It is not yet six o'clock, and as we have just had the opinion of one layman, permit me to give the opinion of another layman. We have listened to lawyers all the afternoon, and the whole question simmers down to this : If Mr. Loy is a liar and a perjurer, then the gentlemen opposite are right; but if he is an honest man, as I believe he is, then they are wrong. I believe Loy is honest, and I am going to support the report of the majority.

MCCARTHY (North Simcoe) moved third reading of Bill (No. 64) to incorporate the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company.

FOWLER (King's, N.B.) Mr. Speaker, before this motion passes I wish, pursuant to the notice which I have given, to move :
That the said Bill be referred back to the Committee of the Whole, with instructions that they have power to amend the .same by providing that a branch line be built from the proposed main trunk line of the Grand Trunk Mr. OSLER.
Pacific Railway, beginning at a point at or near where said trunk line crosses the Nuskwaak river, and thence extending, by way of Fredericton and the valley of the St. John river, to St. John city.
It is not necessary for me at this time to go into this matter at any length, as it was discussed to a considerable extent when the Bill was in Committee of the Whole. I think this is a very important provision. As was pointed out at that time, it would be impossible for the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Pacific Company to enter into an arrangement by which a portion, and even the whole of the common stock of the new company might be handed over en bloc to the Grand Trunk Railway Company in exchange for certain privileges granted by that company to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. It was also pointed out that this might have a very important bearing upon the freight rates that would be charged by the Grand Trunk Pacific in the territory over which it is to run; that, if the adjustment of the freight rates of the new company were to come before the railway commission which is to be appointed, the amount of the capital stock of the company would be a very important consideration with the commission in estimating what those freight rates should properly be. Therefore, it seems to me important that due provision should be made that no such arrangement as that which I have pointed out should be allowed to take place, but that whatever capital is placed upon the market or is passed from the control of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company to other holders, whether they be private persons or the Grand Trunk Railway Company, should be passed for a money consideration; so that the actual money cost of the Grand Trunk Pacific would be the only thing to be taken into consideration by the commissioners should they be called upon to adjust the freight rates over that road. It may he said that they would still have power to inquire into this matter and to ascertain whether money had been paid for the stock or not; but then, supposing that this stock or a portion of it were to get into the hands of third parties, innocent persons who had paid par for the stock, although the original owners of it had got it for ten or twenty or thirty per cent, or any other figure under par, it would not be fair to these innocent holders of the stock not to take into consideration the amount they had paid for it. I do not intend to make any extended remarks on this matter. The thing seems to me to be so plain that I cannot understand how any member of this House can oppose my amendment.

Mr. Speaker, when the government's proposal in relation to the Grand Trunk Pacific was introduced into the House, the Prime Minister stated that he would insist that the

Grand Trunk should acquire $25,000,000 of this stock; and I think he ought to tell the House and the country how he intended that the Grand Trunk Company should acquire that stock-whether by purchase or by what means ?

While we are waiting for the answer of the right hon. First Minister, I may point out that it is provided in the contract that the Grand Trunk Company shall acquire this stock. What we want to know is in what way it is proposed that they shall acquire it ?

Of course, the amendment of the hon. member for King's, N.B. (Mr. Fowler), is something which is absolutely unprecedented. Not one precedent has been cited where a clause was ever inserted in a charter requiring a company to sell its stock for any given sum of money. The question which has been asked the Prime Minister, of course, I cannot answer more than to say that I do not see how such a question can reasonably be asked, namely, how a company which acquires stock shall acquire it. I suppose they will acquire it in the course of business, according to the law of the contract, which must be construed in accordance with the law of the land. In that contract the government require the Grand Trunk Railway Company to acquire $25,000,000 of this stock. Personally speaking, I think that was a wise precaution. It was, at all events, an answer to the criticism that the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada was not behind or aiding or assisting in the scheme of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. The Grand Trunk Railway Company, when they do acquire this stock, are bound to hold it for fifty years and possibly longer-at all events, until the bonds which the government have guaranteed are paid off. The company cannot dispose of that stock, but must hold it as a guarantee that they are interested in and are behind this scheme. But that we Should insert in a charter a clause that a certain stock shall be sold for cash at par value, is something which I never yet knew to be asked to be inserted in any other charter which has ever passed this House.

I made that inquiry because I regard it as a matter of importance. That provision is put in the contract for some specific purpose. I assume that it is for the purpose of establishing confidence in the public mind, that this transaction is a bona fide one, and that the provision made for security is all that could be desired. For what purpose is it made compulsory on this company to secure it, if it is not some ^guarantee that the Grand Trunk Railway will have an interest in this undertaking which will' compel them to carry it out. The hon. member for North Simcoe says that this is an unprecedented thing. It is, but he must remember

Mr. McCarthy. I do not say that the question of contract is unprecedented because two parties to a contract may agree on anything ; but speaking of the charter, I say it is unprecedented to insert in a charter a provision requiring the stock of the company to be sold at a particular price.

While that may be unprecedented, the intention of parliament is to provide that this stock shall be taken up In order to furnish a guarantee. We have never had to deal with such a Bill before. Here are two corporations, and the same men are on the directorate of each. We are giving the directors of the one company the power to sell to themselves, as directors of the other company, a certain amount of stock and at whatever price they like. The directorate may sell it to the other at five cents in the dollar. Will any one say that such a transfer as that would be any guarantee for the carrying out of the undertaking ? This provision looks very like a blind to the public, an attempt to make the public believe that there is some kind of guarantee because we compel the Grand Trunk Railway to take $25,000,000 worth of stock in the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, whereas the fact is that since the same men are on the directorate of both companies, the one board may sell the stock to the other at five cents on the dollar. That being the case, is it unreasonable that we should provide that if the Grand Trunk Railway purchase the stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, they must give some substantial consideration for it. Prime Minister that the clause in its unamended form is a substantial guarantee.

It is contended by supporters of the government, by the government press, that this provision furnishes a substantial guarantee to the country that the Grand Trunk Railway are behind the scheme and will carry it out. It is one that the people will not regard as a proper contract to be passed by this House.

Before the question is put, we should have a declaration from the government with regard to this matter. Does the government attach any special importance to the fact that the Grand Trunk Railway is required to acquire $25,000,000 of the common stock of this company ? I think that that is a perfectly fair question to submit to the government at this time, and for these reasons.

It is said that the Grand Trunk Railway is behind this company, and that the fact that it will control the common stock is a source of strength to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. In what way is that a source of strength ? Does the government take the position that it is a source of strength to this company that the Grand Trunk Railway should acquire this stock for a nominal consideration ? If that is the attitude of the government, I am not supposed to agree with it. For it would only result in an excessive capitalization of the company; and, in the end, might prove an obstacle in the way of controlling the rates as we should control them in the interest of shippers. Then, there is another matter in this connection as to which, I think, we ought to have some answer. The clause which is dealt with by the motion proposed by my hon. friend from King's, N.B. It may he that, in the future, it will be desirable to provide otherwise. But we are dealing with the provisions of the law as they are to-day, and as they have been for many years past. Now, I come to the main point made by my hon. friend. If the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada acquire this stock, why should they be treated differently from any other purchaser of the stock ? For, practically, that is what this amendment means. My hon. friend has said, and has said rightly, that the government attaches great importance to the Grand Trunk Railway Company coming
into this scheme and standing behind it. The government in that, I think, interprets rightly the feeling of the Canadian people generally. They would he more confident of the ability of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway to cope with the enterprise if that company have the backing of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada. And I hold, that instead of being deterred from taking part in this scheme, the Grand Trunk Railway Company should be encouraged to stand behind it, because by so doing they will be of great assistance in the successful carrying out of the enterprise. But, if the Grand Trunk Railway Company are to come into the scheme, is there any reason why they should be subjected to more severe obligations than any other purchaser of the common stock of the company ? So far the words as they were in the Act of 1888, and as they were in clause 12 of the Bill as introduced into this Hiouse. What follows then ?
Or as consideration for rights, powers and privileges acquired.
Now, those are very important words. We must not forget that the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada have practically one set of directors. They are different in name, I know, the former has some senators, for example, that are not in the Grand Trunk Railway Company, but we understand they are going to disappear. Nobody doubts that the directorial power iu the two companies will be practically and in effect the same. Now, these two Mr. BARKER.
companies with one board of directors, one power, one government, will meet to do- what ? To enter into agreements for traffic arrangements between the companies under the powers of the general Railway Act. They can agree there in consideration of the terminal facilities which the Grand Trunk Railway Company may give to this new company, to give any consideration whatever, however large ; and under these little innocent looking words the whole $25,000,000 of stock may be given as a consideration for the interchange of traffic between these two companies, when, according to the right hon. gentleman, it is a part of the undertaking, without compensation, that the Grand Trunk Railway is going to help this road and be behind it. Out of the forty-five millions of capital, the Grand Trunk evidently intends-or there is no object in putting that clause in the Bill-evidently intends to get twenty-five millions of paid-up stock, and everybody knows that the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada cannot pay that amount of money for it.
Mr, MCCARTHY. Does the hon. gentleman appreciate the fact that the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada has got to hold this stock in its entirety for fifty years?

Yes, but the company are to rank as stockholders, and it will be paid-up stock, and when you come by and by to settle tariffs, you will hear of this to the cost of this country. That is the objection. Let the Grand Trunk pay in hard cash as holders of the twenty-five millions, and we will know where we are. But the country does not want to pay tolls in respect of this stock given to the Grand Trunk for the interchange of traffic. That is the contention here, and it is for that reason that the hon. gentleman from King's (Mr. Fowler) wishes to make it quite clear that the stock subscribed for by the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall be paid for in cash, so that hereafter it will he known what they did pay for it and what the company got for it.

Although I have spoken once before, perhaps I may be allowed to reply to an observation of the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker). He knows tliis better than I do, because he is an authority on railways, and he does not pretend, surely, that because we print in the Bill a limit of the capital stock at forty-five million dollars, that we are hound to take that amount into consideration when we consider the rates. It seems to be in the mind of the hon. gentlemen opposite that we shall have to take Into computation of the freight rates the forty-five million of dollars, whatever has been paid for it. If the Grand Trunk Railway Company do issue forty-five millions of stock and if they pay twenty-five millions, all that will he taken into consideration in fixing the rates will he the twenty millions, and not the

forty-five millions. Therefore,, it does not matter what they are authorized to pay ; what matters it that they shall pay the fail-value of the stock, and whatever they pay shall be the basis of the rate to be levied upon shippers. '

I am very well aware of what the right hon. gentleman has said. But the right hon. gentleman knows that he is enabling these two companies to agree between themselves what the value may be of the privileges and rights accorded under this agreement; and ten years hence no commissioners, parliament, or anybody else, can go back upon that and say whether the value they put upon that agreement is or is not correct. But if you require the cash, you will know where you are. That is the distinction. Suppose, for example, that to-morrow these two companies were to sit down together-the same body of gentlemen perhaps, though really acting as two distinct corporations-and they agree that the Grand Trunk shall give terminal facilities to the Grand Trunk Pacific in Montreal or at other points, and they estimate between themselves that such facilities are worth an enormous sum of money, and in consideration of those facilities they issue paid-up stock, who hereafter is going to say that that was not the true value ? How are you going to get at it ? If you make it a eash basis, you will know what cash went into the company, and then it will be quite correct, as the hon. gentleman says, that if only twenty millions were paid in, that is all they could reckon in the settlement of the tariff or the tolls. But when you enter into such arrangements as are referred to here, compensation for rights, powers and privileges, who hereafter is going to measure the value of those rights and powers ? The right hon. gentleman leaves the whole thing at large, and it is impossible hereafter to say whether the stock issued, whether this twenty-five millions or forty-five millions, ought or ought not to stand for its full value in the settlement of tolls.
Amendment (Mr. Fowler) negatived on division.

I desire to move :
That the Bill be not now read the third time but that It be referred hack to the Committee of the Whole, with instructions to amend section twelve by omitting the word * Graven-hursit ' therefrom.
I desire to amend section 12 by the omission of the word * Gravenhurst ' or, at all events in such a way as not to give the company a roaming commission to establish branch lines from both North Bay and Gravenhurst. If we were to say from North Bay instead of Gravenhurst I would be satisfied, or from Gravenhurst instead of North Bay I would also be satisfied, but I do not think in the interest of other companies that have undertaken the construc-253
tion of roads in that locality it would be proper to give a roving commission to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. I trust the promoter of the Bill will accept the amendment and confine it either to Gravenhurst or North Bay.
Amendment (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) negatived.

I desire to move an amendment of which I gave notice some time ago and which is as follows
That Bill (No. 64) be not now read the third time buit that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole House for the purpose of amending section eight by adding thereto the following words ' The majority of the directors of whom the presidemt shall be one shall be British subjects.'
This clause was inserted in the agreement with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and it seems to me that it was a wise precaution. I hope that the hon. gentleman who has charge of this Bill (Mr. McCarthy) will see his way clear to accepting this amendment. About a year ago we had a good deal of talk In this country In reference to the stock of the Canadian Pacific Railway becoming so absorbed by those interested In American railway systems that the Canadian Pacific Railway might practically become an American institution. However, that was guarded against by the fact that the majority of the directors of the Canadian Pacific Railway are British subjects. It will be a very serious thiug, It seems to me, if any of our transcontinental railways were to be placed under the control of the powerful syndicates which are operating and which are at the head of American railway systems. It would have a tendency to build up United States cities and ports at the expense of Canadian cities and ports. Under these circumstances they could operate, if they saw fit, Canadian roads in favour of the United States and against domestic enterprises and it seems to me that this would be a restriction against the adoption of such a policy. I would ask the promoter of this Bill to accept this amendment.

If my hon. friend (Mr. Kemp) will accept a suggestion I would say that while I think his amendment is a good one and I do not see any objection to it, I think we had better introduce it Into the Bill confirming the contract which will come later. I am prepared to accept this amendment, but I think it would be better to put it into the Bill confirming the contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company.
I understand the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Banner) to say that this provision will be made a part of the contract V

Yes.



Amendment (Mr. Kemp) withdrawn.

That the Bill be not now read the third time but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole, with instructions that they have power to amend the same by providing that a branch line be put from the proposed main trunk line of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, beginning at a point at or near where said trunk line crosses the Nashwaak river, and thence extending, by way of Fredericton and the valiley of the St. John river, to St. John city.
Mr. McCarthy. I would like the ruling of the Speaker as to whether an hon. gentleman can move a motion of which another hon. gentleman has given notice.
I gave my reasons in opposition to the proposed line laid down in the Bill
Order, order. The hon. gentleman has not given notice.

1 cannot lay my hand just now on the authority, but I am sure to have seen somewhere in May that a motion making an important amendment to a private Bill must be moved by the hon. member giving notice of it. I cannot just now lay my hand upon the authority but I am pretty sure that the amendment can be moved only by the hon. gentleman who has given notice of it.
Mr. Speaker, the ground I take
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) has spoken once.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. McCarthy) has spoken forty times and I am satisfied that if he will only have the goodness to keep quiet the business of the House will proceed much better. I am asking a question in reference to a point of order and if I am not within my rights 1 will be delighted to obey the rules of the House. In case this Bill passes nine o'clock, notice can again be given and the member giving notice can move the motion.
That is not a notice; it is a suggestion.

I understood that having already spoken on the motion of which I gave notice it was against the rules of the House for me to move the second motion of which I gave notice. I would like to ask the Speaker's ruling on the point as to whether it is in order to move this motion. If it is I am sure I will be delighted to do so and to discuss the question too.

It will have to be done with the unanimous consent of the House. T understand the House agrees to that.
Mx-. FOWLER. Well then, I beg to move, pursuant to notice that I have already given :

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That this Bill he not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole, with instructions that they have power to amend the same by providing that a branch line be built from the proposed main trunk line of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, beginning at a point at or near where said trunk line crosses the Nas.hwaak river, and thence extending, by way of Fredericton and the valley of the St. John river, to St. John city.
There was some discussiou the other evening when this Bill was before the Committee of the Whole in respect to this branch line. The charter as first introduced does not provide for any branch extending from the main line to the city of St. John. I brought the matter up and requested the promoter of the Bill to make such an amendment to the Bill as would provide for a direct connection with the city of St. John. Without such direct connection, in order to reach the largest Atlantic seaport of Canada it would be necessary to go round by way of Moncton which was the proposed terminus of this so-called-this so-called-1 say it advisedly-transcontinental road. Transcontinental as applied to a road which it is proposed shall stretch from one ocean to the other but which stops at an inland town seems rather a misnomer. It was-not, by the charter as originally introduced, proposed to make any connection at all with the city of St. John which is the largest, city in the province of New Brunswick, and which is the nearest Atlantic port on the Canadian coast. I consider that this was a very serious blunder on the part of those who are promoting the Bill. I ask that the Bill be amended to the extent that the city of St. John will have direct connection by the shortest possible route with the main trunk line. There was a counter proposition by the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson), who proposed that instead of going by the shortest and most direct route from the main trunk line of the proposed road, we should go by a more roundabout way, around by the small country toiyn of Chipman and thence to Norton, a point on the line of the Intercolonial Railway between Moncton and St. John, and about 83 miles from St. John. Now, even by the contention of the hon. member (Mr. Emmerson) this proposed course would be considerably longer than the proposition which I make in this motion now before the House. It was very easy matter to take the map of any country and sit down with a pencil and draw lines which shall be short routes. The hon. member for Westmoreland is either oblivious of the fact, or he has forgotten it if he ever knew it, that the route which he proposes for this main trunk line is through thie most mountainous part of the province of New Brunswick. It is through a part of the province which is not only very rugged aud mountainous, but which abounds in lakes of considerable size, and

in order to avoid these lakes-because even this Grand Trunk Pacific Railway road will scarcely be able to run on the water- in order to avoid these lakes and to get a feasible pass through these mountains, it will be necessary to make wide detours. And when that is taken into consideration and the necessary allowance made for these wide detours, the route which is proposed by the hon. gentleman will be more than 50 miles longer than the route followed, say from Edmundston, where it should come really, down the valley of the St. John river to the city of St. John. I do not know w*hy this town of Moncton was made the terminus of the road. If it were intended to get the shortest possible route to the Atlantic seaboard it certainly was a very great mistake to make the town of Moncton that terminus.
Nine o'clock.
The hour for private Bills having expired, the House will resume the consideration of the motion of Mr. Wade, and the amendment thereto.

maintopic: INDEPENDENCE OF PARLIAMENT- MR. LOY, M.P.
speechtext:
When the debate began this afternoon I did not intend to speak upon the question, as in common with many other members of the House, owing to the fact that the evidence of the committee had not been printed, I had not been able to acquaint myself so fully with the facts as I would desire. But in the course of the discussion certain matters have transpired and certain statements have been made which I think should not go unchallenged. It has been stated this afternoon that the majority of those who have spoken on both sides of the House are lawyers, and this one would anticipate in a question of this kind. One of the laymen who spoke (Mr. Heyd) on behalf of the hon. member for Beauharnois, said that if lawyers could not agree upon a statement of the law how then would Mr. Loy be expected to know the law? Well, I do not wish to press this point, but their are certain recognized rules of law which have to be adopted in order that justice shall prevail, and one of them is that ignorance of the law is no excuse. In other words, the hon. member whose seat is attacked, whether he did or did not know the law relating to his case, is bound in common with all the subjects of the King by the law as it exists. Otherwise it would be impossible in many instances to carry out the just provisions of the law. But I am not going to address the House to-night so much upon the question of whether the seat of the hon. member should or should not be va-253$
cated, as to reply to certain very broad! statements made by at least two members of the legal profession who spoke on the government side. It has been recognized since courts of justice have been known in Britain and in this country, that that which you cannot do directly as being a violation of the law, you cannot do by any underhand method; you cannot by a trick evade the law and so evade the responsibility which attaches to violation of the express provisions of the law. It is also well recognized that if certain circumstances exist which would put a man of ordinary prudence and discretion upon inquiry, and if the courts find that inquiry was avoided, much more so if it is found that the party deliberately closed his eyes so as to avoid a knowledge of that which would be prejudicial to him or inconvenient for him to know; then the same consequences must attach as if he had actually known all the circumstances. It is, therefore, exceedingly pertinent and important in dealing with this question that we should come to a conclusion not only as to whether the member for Beauharnois had actual knowledge by words or by letter of tile circumstances which were transpiring in reference to his property; but it is pertinent and important to inquire whether the surrounding circumstances were such as would carry conviction and would suggest inquiry to any reasonable man situated as he was at that time. I merely refer to this. But I am induced to speak for a few^ minutes upon this question more particularly because of certain broad propositions, of law particularly, and some statements of fact made, this afternoon by the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) and the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt). The former gentleman, concluded his argument in these words:	' A certain class of lawyers '
-and he did not finish them. I was rather puzzled why he did not explain what this term meant. I cannot explain it unless he had in mind a certain class of lawyers who when) they have a poor case, usually abuse the opposite counsel. If he had, I do not know that that reference is borne out by the fact. If he refers to the hon. gentleman on this side of the House who brought up this matter, I do not find that the hon. gentleman abused anybody. On the contrary, I think the consensus of opinion in this House must be that he presented the matter in a calm and temperate way, with that proper measure of judicial discretion and that observance of judicial rules which we would expect in a matter of this importance, involving very grave issues to the hon. member for Beauharnois. But on the other hand, although it is true that there are certain circumstances in which a lawyer displays the fact that he has a weak case by abusing the opposite counsel, there is another way of determining whether a

counsel has the conviction that he hasi not a strong case, or whether or not he has a strong ease. When we find the Chairman of the Committee on Privileges and Elections, the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) and the hon. junior member for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt), men of such a very high legal standing in this country, men of such conspicuous ability, men of such great fame in the profession-when we find these gentlemen struggling with this case for so long a time, with the result that as they proceed with their argument it becomes darker for the member for Beauhar-nois, what do we think then of the case ? Is there not a suggestion that the case as presented by these hon. gentlemen is not strong ? Can we come to any other conclusion than that if these hon. gentlemen, with their well known forensic skill, had a good strong case, they would make a very powerful argument ? Now, I will not say on behalf of the hon. gentleman whose seat is attacked, ' save me from my friends,' because that might imply something not very complimentary to the hon. gentlemen who are assisting him ; but I will for the moment address myself to a statement made by the hon. member for Annapolis. He said, if I understood him aright, that Mr. Johnston sold to the government, and that if lie did, having made a valid contract with the sitting member for Beauharnois, then the sale was valid. I dispute the proposition that Mr. Johnston sold to the government. What are the facts ? The facts ns stated by the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte), and not questioned by any member of this House, are that he instructed a gentleman in Montreal, Mr. Dan

durand, to purchase this property for the purpose of a post office site; that this gentleman went to Mr. Johnston and instructed him to act in the matter ; that Mr. Johnston says that, acting upon that instruction, he went to Valleyfieid and made an arrangement with the sitting member to secure an ojftion for the purchase of this property. He was in league with the government. He had no money with which to purchase the property. He never changed his position. He began as an agent of the government-a sub-agent, it is true, but his position is not modified by that circumstance-and continued to negotiate as an agent of the government. He was supplied through the agency of a gentleman; whom the ex-Minister of Public Works had instructed to act on behalf of the government. So it is impossible to argue that this gentleman was In any sense purchasing on his own behalf. From"first to last he was purchasing ns the professed agent of the government, under instructions directly given through the Department of Public Works, with money which was procured through the agency of the government; and he was paid as an agent by receiving afterwards the sum of Mr. LENNOX.
$300 through the abatement made by the vendor of the property and $100, which I think was contributed by the government. The letter which was sent, stating that the government required certain land, is important as showing whether or not the hon. member for Beauharnois had a knowledge of the fact before the transaction was consummated that the property was to be the property of the government. Now, it was admitted by the hon. member for Annapolis that if, as a matter of fact, the hon. member for Beauharnois knew that the government was to be the purchaser, and that Johnston was virtually only an agent before the transaction was consummated by a deed of the property, then the law must apply and the seat must be vacated, as the hon. member had violated the law. What is the evidence on this point ? It is suggested by the hon. leader of the opposition, with that fairness which characterizes that hon. gentleman that probably that letter in itself was not altogether conclusive ; that it might be subject to the interpretation that Mr. Loy understood that he was carrying out the transaction with Johnston, and that Johnston was entering into an independent transaction with the government. But having regard to the facts and to the question which was put by Mr. Loy at the time the negotiation for the purchase was entered into, ' Is this for the government ? ' having regard to the fact that it was notorious that this property above all others was a suitable site for the post office ; having regard to the fact that the hon. member for Beauharnois had been the mayor of that town, and that he was prominently connected with the municipal affairs as well as a parliamentary light: having regard to the additional fact that he was a prominent man, to whom such a question would naturally be communicated, and who would be in touch with the prevailing sentiment of the locality, which is said to have been that his property was the most suitable site for the post office, it is almost inconceivable that he should not have known from that letter that the government intended acquiring his property. At any rate, as he knew all the-circumstances, he was put upon inquiry ; and if he deliberately closed his eyes, he was just as much responsible as if he had allowed the full light to flow in upon him. Then is it consistent with the contention that Mr. Johnston was regarded by the hon. member from Beauharnois (Mr. Loy) as a man of means acting for himself, when just about the time the transaction was being completed by the deed, there was an arrangement made by which an abatement of $300 was taken off the original price upon the ground that he could not otherwise carry out the purchase. Mr. Johnston insisted upon a reduction in the price. Did not that reduction annul the option and make a new contract ? If so, then

the hon. member for Beauharnois was no longer bound by the option he had given. My hon. friend from Annapolis (Mr. Wade) says he does not regard that abatement as constituting a new contract. I shall not question the sincerity of my hon. friend. I take it that he gives us his opinions as an lion, member of this House belonging to the legal profession, candidly and fairly, but I do venture, with all due deference to my hon. friend, to question the soundness of his conclusion. In dealing with this matter, we are not discussing abstract, cast iron rules of law. I understand that we are to apply to it reasonable interpretation upon broad and common sense principles, and I submit that when Mr. Johnston said lie could not carry out the option unless he were given an abatement .of S300, a new contract was then proposed, and my hon. friend from Beauharnois, who then knew that the property was to be transferred to the government, should have declined to conclude the sale. My hon. friend from Annapolis (Mr. Wade) has laid down tiie proposition that if Mr. Loy knew, before the completion of the contract, that the property was going to the government, then the independence of parliament Act applied. Well, having regard to what has transpired, can there be any doubt in the minds of hon. members that the hon. member for Beauharnois must have had at least a very strong suspicion that it was the government which was acquiring the site. Seeing this the hon. the junior member for Ottawa, Mr. Belcourt, took the position that Mr. Johnston did not know that he was purchasing the property for the site of a post office. I had not the opportunity of attending all the meetings of the committee, but 1 was at some of the meetings, and consequently it would be easier for me to carry in my mind the evidence that transpired while I was present than if I had been present at all the meetings. I have a distinct recollection of the examination of Mr. Johnston, and 1 clearly recollect that he explained that he had been instructed to obtain a site for a post office. And what did seem extraordinary to many members of the committee was that he did not stop there, but went on to say that the selection of the site was left to his discretion. Hon. members who were present at that meeting were no doubt as much startled by that evidence as I was. I repeated it immediately afterwards to some members outside, and expressed my astonishment that the choice of a site should have been left to him, Mr. Johnston, the agent of the government. He went to Valleyfield for the purpose of obtaining an option on a site for the post office, and the government, through Mr. Dandurand, provided him with the money to carry out the sale. The hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt) cited to us article 1472 of the Quebec Civil Code. I recognize no substantial difference between that
article and the law in the province of Ontario. That article reads :
Sals is a contract by which one party gives a thing to the other for a price in money which the latter obliges himself to pay for it.
Let me draw attention to these words : ' Which the latter obliges himself to pay for it. They are not at all unimportant in the consideration of this matter, because an option differs very substantially from an ordinary contract of sale, In which both parties are mutually obligated, the option of sale being more in the nature of a mere offer. Now the portion of this article of the code to which my hon. friend wished to direct attention is this :
It is perfected by the consent alone of the parties, although the thing sold be not then delivered.
I quite agree with my hon. friend that this is a good proposition in law, not only in the province of Quebec, but probably throughout the Dominion generally. But if a sale is perfected by consent, it is only perfected within the terms of the written document or within the terms of consent. It is contended by my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt) that the whole matter is to be determined by the condition of things as we find them on the 16th of July. I need not remind hon. members who are of the legal profession only, for it is well known to all the members of this House, that fraud in the initiation of a contract vitiates it, that no contract founded in fraud or misrepresentation can be enforced at the suit of the person who is a party to the fraudulent misrepresentation. Specific performance, indeed ! At whose Suit ? Could there be specific performance at the suit of Johnston ? Why, he went there with a deliberate falsehood in his mouth. He went there instructed to make statements that were untrue. The sitting member for Beauharnois was a public man, interested in the welfare of his town. It was a matter of interest to him whether that property should be used for some great public purpose, such as suplying a need of the town of Valleyfleld. or should be diverted to some other purpose. The representation made that the property was being purchased for a purpose other than that which was actually stated would have met Johnston immediately if he came into court for specific performance. Could specific performance have been enforced at the suit of the Crown ? What position was the Crown in ? I call attention of the members of the government to that. The Minister of Public Works, who has charge of this matter, holding that the property was desirable in the interest of the government and in the interest of the country, formed a plan by which to acquire it. He goes to an agent and the agent employs a sub-agent, who is instructed to misrepresent to the vendor what the

property is to be used for. So, the Crown, which we are supposing to have instituted proceedings, is shown to have been aware that this property could not have been bought directly by fair and open dealing from the sitting member for Beauharnois, and yet it comes into court and asks for specific performance of the contract. What will the answer of the court be? The answer will be: This matter did not begin on a fair and open basis; and, in addition, the government of Canada, who, above all parties, should not initiate a suit directly contrary to public policy and to the words of the statute, cannot say that specific performance should be enforced for the sale of the property of a member of parliament to the Crown. At the suit of Mr. Coy, can specific performance be obtained? I submit to you, Sir, and I feel I am submitting a matter that you will concur in, that no such suit could be successful. X admit that if the contention of the hon. member for Ottawa were correct and the transaction were closed on the 16th July, that the option of sale concludes the whole matter, then there would be good ground. Or. if the suit arose before there was any disclosure made to the sitting member for Beauharnois, then there would be good ground for the suit. But when the facts are that he does know before the time the deed is demanded that the proposal is substantially to vest his property in the Crown, by sale, he being a member of parliament, and in the face of the Act which declares that no sale can be made and no contract entered into between a member of parliament and the Crown, it goes without argument that he too will be denied the remedy of specific performance. What is the remedy, if any? The remedy is to go after Johnston. The remedy is in damages and for damages alone ; and so, section 1077 of the Code, which my hon. friend has cited, comes in very properly. Go after Johnston, the party with whom you dealt, and who deceived you. That is the remedy. It may be said that this is rather hard : it may be said that Johnston is a man of no substance. I have nothing to controvert that. It is probable he is a man of no substance, for it is generally a man of no substance who is put forward to carry out a scheme of this kind. The answer is : Have a care before you enter into contracts with men unknown to you; have a care when a stranger invades your town, and, with some unusual story, asks you t.o bind yourself to sell your property to him, trusting that you will conform to his wishes with all the innocence of youth. But, if with the unsuspicious nature that characterizes the ordinary member of parliament, you sell property of this character, which is kn*wn to be prized by the Dominion government, known to be the only site for an intended post office in your town, it is incumbent upon you to know the man you are Mr. LENNOX.
dealing with, and you have no complaint if you are compelled to seek damages against a worthless man. But. aside from these general propositions which, I say with all fearlessness will be acknowledged by every member of this House as applied to the parties to the contract, there are certain well known rules of courts of equity which must be recognized. A court of equity does not decree specific performance as a matter of course; it decrees it or withholds it at its discretion. I cannot grant the exceptional and peculiar remedy of specific performance except where the righteousness of it is established. He who comes into equity must do equity. The party who claims specific performance must show that his hands are clean, must show that he is guilty of no connivance, no fraud, no questionable conduct. Could any of the parties show this ? But the party who seeks a decree in equity must do more than that. He must show that it is not contrary to public policy. Can this be done in this case? There could be no more flagrant violation of the requirements of public policy than for a court of this land to decree specific performance once they knew that this transaction, on the fact of it honest, was in fact an evasion of the statute, by which evasion the property of a member of parliament would become vested in the Crown represented by gentlemen in political affinity with him who was the vendor of the property.
Now, I want to appeal, not to my friends on this side of the House, but to you, Mr. Speaker, to all members of the cabinet and supporters of the government, on behalf of Mr. Loy. I do not think the hon. member for Beauharnois-I say it in all sincerity- has been treated fairly in this matter. I do not think the government have given the hon. gentleman a fair chance for his life, because, after all, a man's blameless and unblemished reputation is of more value to him than life itself. What is the position in which the government has placed the hon. member for Beauharnois ? It has forced him into this position, than at best he has to stand with a cloud of suspicion attaching to him. If that evidence had been printed, as it was the duty of the government to print it, we could have gone into the discussion of the matter fully and fairly, recognizing that whatever our political differences may be, it is our duty in all honour and in all fairness to stand by each other in that which is right. We would have been able, perhaps, not only to exonerate Mr. Loy from the charges made against him, to the extent of enabling him to hold his seat, but we would have been able, perhaps, so to vindicate his honour as that the whole House would unanimously agree that he was not to blame at all. That might have been the case if the government had allowed the evidence to be printed. But what position are we in ? We are in this

deplorable position, and 1 bope it is not a precedent that will be honoured in the future, that members on this side of the House and on that side of the House cannot agree because they do not know the evidence. It is impossible for hon. gentlemen upon either side of the House, except those who continuously attended the committee-and very few of them did so-to be able to judge of the merits of this case as fully as they ought to be, because they are not possessed of the evidence.
Now, in view of all these circumstances, I am not going to say that I would not like unduly to press the case against the hon. member for Beauharnois, who has been so badly treated by his own friends. They have left him-and don't you forget it-they have left him covered by suspicion, by reason of the notoriety of the fact that the government wanted this property, suspicion by reason of the fact that an appropriation had been made, the suspicious movements of Mr. Johnston in acquiring the property, suspicion by reason of the fact that Loy was a supporter of the government, and that he was specially interested and charged with a knowledge of the whole matter as representative of the city, and by reason of the fact that after the option had expired, and at a time when you would have expected him to be on the alert in regard to a man unknown to him like Mr. Johnston, he appeared indifferent to the result. I say all these circumstances are calculated to cast suspicion upon the conduct of the member for Beauharnois', even though they do not amount to actual proof. Now, under these cricumstances, feeling that the hon. member may well exclaim, ' Save me from my friends,' speaking for myself alone, having no instructions from anybody, having no knowledge of the general opinion on this side of the House, I would be glad, speaking from my feeling of good nature, if the hon. member who has had charge of this matter could see his way clear not to press his motion to a division. I feel that where honour- is at stake, it is better that several hon. members who may be guilty of some infraction of the law should go unpunished, than that one member should have a stigma cast upon him which by possibility is not deserved.

maintopic: INDEPENDENCE OF PARLIAMENT- MR. LOY, M.P.
speechtext:
After the lengthy discussion that has taken place on this motion, I would not venture to address the House now but for the fact that X have the honour of being a member of that committee to whom was confided the investigation of the charge which has been the subject of discussion this afternoon. I do not wish to be understood by the House or by the country as acquiescing in the majority report which has been brought into the House in regard to this matter, nor do I wish to be understood as assenting to some of the propositions that have been laid down by hon. members
opposite in regard to the construction that is to be placed on the contract between Mr. Loy and Mr. Johnston. The junior member for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt) endeavoured to convince this House that the contract of sale between the member for Beauharnois and Mr. Johnston was consummated on the 16tb day of July, and that after that date, no matter what information the hon. member may have received, it was impossible for him to recede from the contract into which he had entered. Now, Sir, I take issue with the hon. member for Ottawa in that position. It is, I think, a proposition in law that will not be disputed by any lawyer, in fact, it is a proposition of individual right which will be recognized,
I think, by every member of this House, that a person having property to sell, a vendor, so to speak, has a perfect and absolute right to dictate and to state upon what terms his property shall be sold. No matter how ridiculous, or how absurd, or how onerous these conditions may be, he has a perfect right to impose these conditions and a perfect right to insist upon these conditions being performed before he is obliged to part with his property. To apply that principle to the case in hand, the hon. member for Beauharnois in signing the option for the purchase of his property had a perfect right to impose upon the intending purchaser whatever terms he saw fit, and unless these terms were acquiesced in by the intending purchaser he was in no way bound. When an option is given for the sale or purchase of property, unless the identical terms under which that option is given are accepted, there is no binding contract. The option may be conditional as to the time in which the option shall be exercised, it may be conditional as to the manner in which the purchase money shall be paid, or it may be optional as to the state of the title, or it may be optional in many other ways. Whatever the conditions imposed by the vendor are, they must be accepted by the intending purchaser ; otherwise, there is no contract. If the terms of the option are varied in any way by the intending purchaser, then something further is required in order to complete the contract ; in other words, the vendor having received a qualified or conditional acceptance it is for himself to go a step farther and acknowledge or confirm the conditional offer that he has received. It is perfectly apparent in this case that no such third step as that was taken. Only two steps were taken in the formation of this contract, and I desire to call the attention of the House to the exact wording of the option and acceptance. I submit with every confidence to the House that upon a fair and reasonable construction of the option and of the letter of acceptance there never was a contract between these two parties before the money was actually paid over. The terms of the option are that he will sell the property^

the right to buy to be exercised by three o'clock on Wednesday afternoon on the 16th, with this further condition ' the price to be $10,000, payable in cash on day of sale.' If the argument of the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Bel,court) is correct, the sale, according to that hon. gentleman, was completed on the 16th July, when the letter, which he termed ' the letter of acceptance.' was written. I defy any one to find in that so-called letter of acceptance an acceptance of the exact terms contained in this option. There were three things to be done-first, the exercise of the option of the 16tli July ; second, the payment of $10,000 ; and, thirdly, the payment at the time of sale. Now, these are the three conditions that the vendor imposed and had a right to impose. Let us see if these conditions have been accepted by the intending purchaser. Mr. Johnston says : ' I beg to accept your offer.' That part of it is all right, and he did that on the 16th July. But then he goes on to sav that he does not accept the second part as to the payment of the $10,000 on the day of sale, but he puts it in this way :
The price will be paid in cash on title being found satisfactory and deeds executed by you.
An entirely different thing from what the vendor had stated in his option. By the terms stated in the option the intending purchaser was bound to exercise that option in its exact terms, but when we read the acceptance of the 16th July we see that the intending purchaser entirely varies the option given to him by. the vendor. For that reason, I say that there was no contract, that there was no confirmation of that intended acceptance by the vendor ; and for that reason, I submit there never was a binding contract by the option and by the intended letter of acceptance between these two parties, if I am right in that contention, then it leads me one step further. The hon. member for Ottawa argued that because there was a contract, therefore, the hon. member for Beauharnois could not withdraw. If I am right in my contention, there was no contract ; and if that be so, the second part of his argument falls to the ground.. If there was no contract between those two parties, as I submit there was not, then it was perfectly open to the hon. member for Beauharnois at any time after he received that letter of the 16th July to have withdrawn from what had taken place, as the negotiations might eventually end in a contract. I submit that the evidence given before the committee amply justifies me hi saying that the hon. member for Beauharnois had become possessed of the knowledge that the government were really purchasing this property, and the moment lie acquired that knowledge, there being no binding contract between himself and the intending purchaser, It was not only his privilege, but his duty as a member of this House, to have repudiated the whole thing and to Mr. PORTER.
have refused to enter into any further negotiations in regard to it. But that was not the only means of escape, to my mind, that the hon. member for Beauharnois had in regard to this matter, and I quite agree with some of the remarks that were made by the last speaker (Mr. Lennox) in regard to this question. If the hon. member for Beauharnois did not know that this property was being sold to the government, the government certainly knew that this property was being bought from the hon. member for Beauharnois, the government knew that the hon. member for Beauharnois was a member of this House at the time, and it was just as incumbent upon the government to inform the hon. member for Beauharnois of the position in which he was placing himself by going on and completing his contract as it was the duty of the hon. member for Beauharnois to have withdrawn from it when he understood what the character of the contract was. There is a principle of law which is as well recognized as any other principle of law that I know of, and it is that it is just as much a fraud to withhold information that should be imparted as to impart false information to a party with whom you are contracting, and I hold that, while the term ' fraud ' may be too harsh, it was withholding on the part of the government information that it was their bounden duty to impart to the hon. member for Beauharnois to enable him to form a proper judgment upon the matter, and to escape the penalties or the obligations of this statute, which is made to protect the parliament of this country. For these two reasons, then, I differ entirely from hon. gentlemen opposite, because I have come to the conclusion from the evidence, as in fact it has been admitted by hon. members on the other side of the House during this discussion, that at a certain time before the money was actually paid over, the hon. member for Beauharnois did become aware that the government were purchasing this property, and having obtained that know-_ ledge before he was bound to carry out the" contract, or the government being under an obligation to impart that knowledge to him, I submit there was no justification for the hon. member for Beauharnois carrying out the contract, nor is it honest or just for the government to ask their supporters to whitewash him in this matter.
