On resolution 1,

I would like to have some better reasons from the lion. Minister of Justice for these resolutions. If my memory does not deceive me, the Liberal party was more strongly opposed to superannuation, when in opposition, than to anything else. And throughout the country, the people, irrespective of party, are opposed to that sort of thing. They consider that a man ought to pay for his own superannuation, and that the tax-payers should not be taxed in order to pay a superannuation allowance to a man who has lived in luxury while in the public service, and neglected to lay up a competency for ills old age. I represent a rural constituency, and my people are not at all in favour of this policy. There are in that constituency labouring men and mechanics who earn from $300 to $400 per year. Is it fair that these men should be taxed on their small earnings to help pension a judge who has been superannuated on full pay, and who lias enjoyed a salary of from $4,000 to $7,000 a year during the years he was on the bench ? I consider this most unfair. It is not even as if these judges had ever paid anything towards their own superannuation. I give this government the credit of having made some changes in our superannuation system since they came to power. Every civil servant now has to pay into the superannuation fund so much a year, and that money is returned to him with interest at 5 per cent when he is superannuated, or is paid to his family should he die before superannuation. There can be no objection to that, because they are" simply getting back what they have con-

tributed. But there is no reason why the government should tax people to keep men living in luxury with their families, who have never contributed anything to the superannuation fund. I am speaking the sentiments of the people I represent.

I represent myself a farming constituency, where there is probably a greater number of farmers than in my hon. friend's riding, .and I have no hesitation whatever in saying that any man who has served his country thirty years as a judge on the bench is entitled to all the consideration he can get. Many of our judges are giving their services to the country on the bench for a pittance compared to what they would earn at the bar.
And just the opposite too.

In my riding there is a vacancy on the county court bench at present. And there is not a lawyer in the county town who would not take the position at the pay, and it is only a county court judgeship. There are also other gentlemen in other towns who are very anxious to get the position, and the pay is more than the most of them earn at, the bar.

There may be something in what the hon. gentleman has said, but there is also a great deal in what I-have said. The bench has ceased to attract the best men at the bar. My hon. friend will admit that some of the men he knows in Ontario, and whom I know in Quebec, have been on the bench twenty-five and thirty years, and are seventy-five years of age and over, and they are obliged to work on when they have really passed their years of labour, because they cannot afford to retire. In view of the very small salary paid distinguished men on the bench, the least we can do is to give them this retiring allowance.
I notice that judges eighty years of age can be compulsorily retired ?
That only applies to county court judges. The high court judges may retire if they choose, but we cannot compel them.
Why is a county court judge to be compelled to retire at eighty years of age ?
Because experience has shown that when a man has reached the age of eighty, it is time for him to leave the bench.

Does the hon. Minister of Justice know that some men at eighty are as full of vigour and as active in intellect as some men of sixty, I do not think it is necessary to compel a man to retire unless lie is unable to do his work. In the county where I live, the judge, who
has been on the bench fifty years, is full of vigour to-day, and the members of the bar there are not anxious to have him retire, nor is he himself anxious to retire. He is full of experience and probably a far- better judge than any one we could select in his place.
What was the age of Mr. Justice Britton when he was appointed to the Superior Court in Ontario ?
I cannot remember.
About seventy, was it not ?
I have no idea at all.

I would like to observe to my hon. friend from Lennox (Mr. Wilson), who seems to take a different view from that presented in these resolutions, and to object that judges be given pensions, because pensions of some kind are not given other classes of the community, that in all civilized countries, particularly England, the services of judges have been deemed of such a character as to make it advisable for the community at large that they should be provided a pension in their old age. The object is to put judges above temptation, to ensure their dignity and independence, and to make them what they should be, the impartial arbiters of all differences in the community. The idea of giving pensions to judges has never been called into question in this House. Ever since confederation, our judges have been granted pensions.
Are you not increasing the amount ?

No. but we provide that, under special circumstances, -a pension will be given. At present when a judge has served fifteen years, he can, on the mere asking, retire and receive a pension of two-thirds of his salary. This resolution provides that when a judge has served thirty years or has reached the age of seventy and served twenty-five years, or the age of seventy-five and served twenty years, he shall be allowed to retire on full pay. Now, my hon. friend objects to this, as do some other hon. members, that men should not be compulsorily retired. Judges of the county court can be compulsorily retired; judges of the superior court cannot be so retired, but they are given the option after having served thirty years, or after having served twenty years and having attained the age of seventy-five years, or after having served the twenty-five years and attained the age of seventy-five years, of withdrawing with full salary. For my part, I am sorry we have not the power to retire even judges of the superior courts compulsorily at a certain age. Such power

of compulsory retirement should not be taken as a reflection upon anybody. Unfortunately, we have to admit that as time goes on our forces diminish. And judges, being human like the rest of us, when they reach a certain age, say seventy-five or eighty years, ordinarily are not as fit as younger men to discharge the important services which the community look to them to render. Take a parallel case, say of generals in the army. In the United States a general is compulsorily retired at sixty-fdur years. In England also, I think, there is a limit of age for the general officers. If I am not mistaken, and speaking under correction, officers in high command are forced, after they have reached a certain limit of age, to take their pensions. The same thing should apply to judges. My hon. friend from West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) speaks of a certain judge who at eighty years of age is as well able to discharge the duties of his position as a man of sixty would be, perhaps better. But exceptions of this kind only prove the general rule, that a man at eighty is not as well fitted to do good work as a judge ns a younger man would be. So, the fact that there is a judge in the county of Elgin who, at eighty years of age is able to discharge his duties proves nothing. Mr. Gladstone at eighty gave perhaps his best services to the state. Those exceptions are very rare. Though my hon. friend (Mr. Robinson) is very vigorous at his age -perhaps sixty, like myself-yet perhaps he will agree with me that his vigour was greater than it is at the present time. I am sorry to be obliged to admit that, as time goes on, our forces, instead of increasing, diminish. This rule of human life is the thing that we have to recognize and provide for in this Bill. It is a painful spectacle which some of those who have to attend in court are compelled to witness -men forced hy reason of the fact that they are not in affluent circumstances, to continue the discharge of duties upon the bench when it is painfully evident that it would be better that they should take their pensions. Then, I repeat, nobody will dispute the fact that the services rendered by the judges are the most important that can be rendered to the country. I think that when a man has discharged his duties as a judge for twenty-five years and has reached the age of seventy-five, or has discharged his duties for thirty years, and, in his own judgment, knows that his forces are diminishing, and it is to the advantage of the public that he should withdraw and make way for younger men, the country should not turn him out on the street, but should maintain him in dignity and affluence and comfort to the end of his days.

I feel as though I would like to die in harness. I do not think it is right, when a servant has been faithful to you all his lifetime and has dis-Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
charged his duty well, to kick him out because he liapens to have his age against him. We all grow old, but we all hate to be kicked out. We would hate to be kicked out even from this House. And if the Prime Minister is able to discharge his duties at eighty years of age, the country would not like to see him kicked out and he would not like it. Here is a judge who has served the country for fifty years and .wishes to continue in his place, and members of the bar who plead before him are nearly all anxious that he should hold the position. It is cruel to turn him out. It is like turning out an old horse in the pasture to die. I hope the minister will make exceptions to this Bill, and, where-ever there is a man capable of discharging his duty to the public, for pity's sake do not turn him out.

I desire to express my own opinion, and the opinion of the class to which I belong-those engaged in mercantile and manufacturing pursuits, who have a great deal of litigation-that it is very desirable that our judges should be amongst the most vigorous of the professional men in the country. I think it is more desirable that a judge should be well paid and should be able to look forward to a pension in old age than that almost any other class that I know of should be in that position. I think that we could do with a different class of politicians, we could even do 'without a great many of those we have, but we cannot do without the best services that our judges can possibly render in a country like this where there is so much litigation. I think, therefore, that the motion before us is absolutely in the right direction. It is impossible for us ail to pay attention to the worthy but sentimental reasons advanced by the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson), because if we do we shall find ourselves in very serious difficulties, such as have been spoken of by the Prime Minister. Judges who are past their best days-and sometimes people, even judges, when they grow old grow obstinate-will not retire when they should. I think it is well that the power afforded by this resolution should be in the hands of the government, so that they may use it in the case of a judge who is not able to perform his duties. It would be invidious, of course, to take a case here and there. It should be made a general rule, and it should be applied, as the Minister of Justice has provided in this resolution. Therefore, I wish to say that I favour the resolution, and I think that, so far as the class to which I belong are concerned, they will be unanimous in support of the government's proposal.

The clause of the resolution under discussion does not make it compulsory for judges of the Supreme or Superior Courts to retire from their posi-

tions, as the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) seems to think. This clause of the resolution only applies to voluntary resignation. And it seems to me that no one can be a better judge of the time when he should retire, and the advantages or disadvantages of retiring than the very men who would be entitled to take advantage of this resolution. A gentleman who has served upon the bench for thirty years and has reached the age limit provided in this resolution, ought to be the very best possible judge as to whether it would be advisable for him to continue in the occupation of his exalted position, or whether it would be to his advantage and to the advantage of litigants and the public generally for him to retire. But, while I think that would be the case, I think it would be unfair, after he had given so many years of service to the country, that a judge should be compelled to retire; or, should he believe that he had become incompetent to discharge the duties of his high office and feel it incumbent upon him to give way to some one else more capable to perform his duties, it is not fair, to my mind, that he should be allowed to retire after spending so many years in the public service without some provision being made by the country he has served faithfully and for so long. For my part, I am in entire accord with the resolution under discussion.
Has the scope of the resolution been taken from any other source, or is it entirely original with ourselves ?

Absolutely original. The only precedent I know of exists in the United States where, with respect to judges of the Supreme Court and judges of the district court of the United States who have served ten years, it is optional with them to retire on full pay, 70 years of age and ten years of service.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax) It seems to me, looking at the scope of the resolution and having regard particularly to the reason suggested by the Prime Minister, that there are possibly some cases not provided for by this resolution and which might deserve consideration. For example, take the case of a judge who is appointed at the age of forty-five years and has served twenty years, and at the age of sixty-five he finds himself subject to some infirmity which greatly interferes with or absolutely prevents the discharge of his duties as a judge. It seems to me that the reasoning of the Prime Minister would include a case of this kind. But the right hon. gentleman will observe that that is a case which is not covered by the terms of this resolution.
Perhaps to meet a case of that kind we might require some medical certificate.

I am assuming that everything of that kind would be safeguarded by such means as would be found desirable in the public interest. I do not know whether cases of that kind have been considered by the government, but in listening to the observations of the right hon. gentleman it struck me that there might be cases of that kind which would, be just as deserving of consideration as those which are dealt with in the resolution.

With these resolutions I entirely agree. I cannot see why they should not be extended to all the judges. If the age limit is to be applied to the lower court judges I do not see why it should not be applied to judges of the higher courts. As the hon. gentleman knows, there are cases where a man reaches his greatest vigour and is more useful at eighty years of age than at sixty. But these cases are very rare. I do not know why exception is made of the Supreme Court and Superior Court judges. It strikes me this provision should be applied to them quite as much if not more than to the lower court judges. I think in that particular the Bill does not go far enough. The Prime Minister truly said that when a man is appointed judge he should be rendered independent of all cares and anxieties as to money, and he should have full provision made for his old age after he has served the country for a long period. After all, I think these provisions do not go to the root of the matter, because the salaries we are paying our judges now were fixed at the time of confederation when living was very much cheaper than it is now. The result is, as the Minister of Justice knows, that to-day it is difficult to get the men we would like to take positions in the higher court. Another result is that we find our judges are more and more endeavouring by other means to implement their salaries. We find the judges in our higher courts, many of our best judges that we all look up to with great confidence, taking positions as directors of various companies, looking out for various outside sources of supplementing their Incomes. I think that is a serious detriment to the administration of justice in Canada, and some way ought to be found of stopping this practice, as I consider it a very serious evil. These judges are sought for by companies whose object It is to get men who will inspire the public with confidence in their concerns. My experience of judges is that as a rule they are not good business men, and I think that statement may be made of judges generally. I would be afraid to say what proportion of them, at all events in Ontario, take positions in companies about the business of which they can really know nothing. They are forced to do so because their incomes are not sufficient for their position. Any lawyer of great ability in large centres like Toronto, or Hamilton, or London, or Mont-

real, or Quebec, or Ottawa, will make a larger income in the practice of his profession than the salaries received by any one of our judges. I think we cannot attain what ought to be our object, that is to have judges who are absolutely independent, until we increase their salaries very materially.

In answer to what has fallen from the hon. gen-leman, I may say that it is not within our power to affect the tenure of office of judges of the high court. Under the British North America Act, section 96, the Governor General has exclusive power of appointing judges of the superior, district and county courts in each province. Section 99 provides that the judges of the superior courts shall held office during good behaviour. So we have absolutely no power to interfere. I must admit that I am one of those who would not like to have power to interfere with the judges of the high courts. I think the more they are kept beyond our control, directly or indirectly, the better it is for the bench and for the public at large. I would like to take advantage of this occasion, when I am endeavouring to do as much as I can for the judges off the high courts, to say that I agree entirely with what has just fallen from the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) when he says that it is not desirable that our judges should be mixed up in commercial corporations. I hold strong views on that subject myself, and I have no doubt about the impropriety of it. I am of the opinion that if a judge is paid a salary to give his whole time to the service of the country ini that position, he has no right to divert any portion of that time to any other purpose. I think that remark applies with great force to those judges who take upon themselves to sit as directors in financial institutions, and to be connected with corporations which take a portion of their time, to the detriment of the interest of the public.

Representing as I do a rural constituency, I would like to say a word with reference to these resolutions, and fori this reason. We have in our constituency a very intelligent, broad-minded and liberal judge, who has passed the age of eighty years. Now we think it is only right that a judge such as this one should be allowed to retire with full allowance and full pay. We are exceedingly anxious that the very best men the country can afford should be placed upon the bench. If there is anything that we are prouder of than another, it is the status which our judges have throughout the length and breadth of the Dominion of Canada. We are exceedingly anxious that conditions may be made such that our best men can take these positions and this resolution enables them when in the natural course of events they are no longer able to perform their duties to retire on a sufficient allowance. In my own Mr. OSLER.
constituency and in other rural constituencies there are men in the ordinary walks of life who are not able to engage counsel in a case which comes before a judge and it is an advantage to have a fair-minded judge who will take the case up for them and see that justice is given to them. This matter has come to the notice of the people in my constituency for the reason that our judge is very advanced in years and he will be able to retire with an allowance if the resolution that is now before the committee is carried out.

I heartily concur in this resolution just as it is. I am not sure that the suggestion of the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) is not one that would probably involve us in difficulty afterwards. If I undertsand aright the provisions of this resolution they are to reward those who have spent a certain number of years in the public service. It might happen in the case suggested by the hon. leader of the opposition that a judge might be incapacitated by illness or by some accident from performing his ordinary judicial duties. Then we would have to be guided by the question of the degree of fitness or unfitness. While we might say of one judge that he was unfitted we might say of another judge that he was unfitted in a lesser degree, and that while we would give a certain benefit to one we would not give the same benefit to another because he was not unfitted to the same degree. I can see that difficulties might arise in regard to that. A judge may have served five or ten years and he may meet with an accident which renders him unfit to perform his duties as a judge. He would then be placed in the same position as a judge who had probably served twenty or twenty-five years, that is if I understand the suggestion aright which has been made by the hon. gentleman. I do not think that is really the intention of this resolution as brought down and if the government were to adopt such a suggestion I take it that they would meet with that difficult}'. I wish to say a word further, not in connection with this resolution, but in connection with judges. In my opinion judges and especially judges of the Supreme Court are underpaid. We certainly want the very best men that we can possibly get at the bar to act as our judges. There is no more important position in the land to fill than that of judge. Judges have in their hands questions as to rights of property between subject, and subject sometimes involving very large sums of money. Therefore, we should have the most honest, the most upright and the most capable men that we possibly can have, men most learned in the law, men possessing judicial minds, and I would like to see some measure brought in by which the salaries of these judges will be increased or a readjustment of the salaries of judges from one end of

Canada to the other made. If they are worthy of the office of judge, then, they are worthy of being paid proper salaries, salaries that will place them beyond any question of suspicion of being tampered with in performing their duties and place them beyond any question of want when their term of office expires or they are obliged to retire by reason of age. I would also say a word in reference to county court judges and particularly the county court judges in the west. For, instance, in that part of the west where I live and practice my profession our county court judge is paid $2,400 per annum. He has not the advantage, as in many places in the east, of being able to receive fees from surrogate work, so that practically all that the judge in Kootenay county, British Columbia, and I take it in other counties in British Columbia has, is the sum of $2,400. That was not a sufficient sum to induce any man who practices at the bar, who has any practice in any town or district in British Columbia to accept a seat on the bench. There should be some-provision by which the salary of these judges should be increased, there should be some fees derived from surrogate work, or they should be allowed a certain amount for living expenses, because living expenses are much higher there than in the east. The salary of our county court judge unaided as it is by fees from outside sources is much less than the salary of county court judges in the east.
Everything is higher out there.

Everything is higher, even most of the men.
Mr. G1LMOUR. Do I understand that this resolution in regard to Supreme Court and Superior Court judges requires that they shall reach a certain age before they are entitled to their retiring allowance ?

Under the law as we have it, a judge immediately after his appointment, if he becomes incapacitated from illness, may retire upon two-thirds of his salary. If he has served fifteen years, at tlie expiration of the fifteenth year he can go off with his pension notwithstanding the fact that he may be in full possession of all liis faculties. In the amendment which I now propose if a judge has reached seventy-five years of age and spent over twenty years on the bench he may retire, or if he has reached the age of seventy years and spent twenty-five years on the bench he* may retire, or if he has served thirty years on the bench he may retire, whatever his age may be.
I think if anything should happen to a judge after five or ten years service he should have some portion of his salary as a retiring allowance.

I was desirous of seeing what safeguard has been provided by the statute in the case which has been referred to by the hon. Minister of Justice, namely, the case of a judge who, having served less than fifteen years, becomes incapable of properly performing his duties, and therefore has to retire.
There is no way of compelling a judge to retire. He must act of hiS own motion.
I understand that thoroughly.
I will send the statute over to my hon. friend.

In reply to what has been suggested by my hon. friend from Yale and Cariboo (Mr. Galliher), of course, I understand that there must be some safeguard, and that you must not adopt any policy that would place any judge under the control of the executive. I would be as much afraid of that as my hon. friend is, but I would like to point out to him that under the law as we have it at present, you have the matter dealt with already in the case of a judge *who not having served for 15 years, nevertheless becomes incapable of performing his duties as judge. 1 will read the section, omitting the immaterial portions :
If any judge of any superior court who becomes afflicted with some permanent infirmity disabling him from the due execution of his office, resigns-his office ; Her Majesty may by letters patent under the great seal, reciting such permanent disability, grant unto such judge an annuity equal to two thirds of the salary annexed to the office he held at the time of his resignation ; to commence immediately after his resignation and to continue henceforth during his natural life.
I am uot at present aware, whether there is any provision in the statute as to ascertaining what the permanent disability is.

A medical certificate.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax.) This is the practice of the Department of Justice, and not a provision of the statute. Of course, that does not provide for the case where the judge becomes incapable of resignation. Then, applying the principle of the law as it is at present to the case I suggested, you would have this condition of affairs perhaps : A judge appointed at the age of 45 years, having served for 20 years, and becoming afflicted with a permanent disability such as is mentioned in this section, would if such a policy commended itself to parliament, retire under the provisions of the statute on a salary equal to that which lie enjoyed at the time of his resignation.

That is what I thought the hon. gentleman was referring to, and that is what struck me as to the 15-year



limit provided for by the statute, and not up to the 25 or 30-year limit; that it seemed clear that if the judge retired from disability such as you mention, you would be practically applying to him the principle of long service, whereas in reality he had not served the full term designated as long service, for instance, the 30 years or 25 years, after attaining a certain age. I can understand his being paid a proportionate part, according to the yearn of service, but not the full amount of the salary such as a long service judge would receive.

I thought my hon. friend (Mr. Galliher) was raising some objection on the ground of the difficulty of ascertaining the permanent disability. 1 was dealing only with that portion of his remarks, and I was pointing out there would be no more difficulty in that case than there is under the provisions of section Id and 15 of chapter 10S of the Revisedi Statutes. Assuming that there is no difficulty of that kind, and there is no more difficulty In the one case than the other, then the other question comes up as to whether or not you have got as strong a case under the circumstances I have suggested for giving to the judge on retirement his full salary, as you have in the cases which are set forth in the resolutions introduced by the Minister of Justice. In the one case you have a man of 70 years of age not afflicted with permanent disability, but retiring on full salary because he has served 25 years. The case I have mentioned seems equally meritorious, namely the case of a judge having attained the age not of 70 years, but 65 years, having served not 25 years, but 20 years, but at the age of 65 becoming afflicted with some permanent disability which would prevent him from performing his judicial duties. It seemed to me, speaking off-hand, that a case of that kind possessed as much merit as the case of a judge who has attained the age of 70 years, and has served 25 years, but who is not afflicted with any permanent disability which should necessitate his retirement.

It would be only a question of whether you have the' two principles ; one the case you have mentioned, and the other the principle of granting a man full pay who would serve the full term. You would have to have a double principle.

That observation of my hon. friend (Mr. Galliher) is perfectly fair and logical. You are, in the case I am suggesting, combining the principle which has been acted on in the statute I have referred to with the principle which is embodied in the resolution of the Minister of Justice. Whether this is a wise and logical thing to do is a question, and I am inclined to think it is wise.
It does seem to me that we should not fix the period of 20 years' service.

1 was only using that by way of illustration.
air. WADE. It does seem to me that a man who goes on the bench and leaves his practice, after he has been on the bench for 10 years and is afflicted by some permanent infirmity, such as blindness or deafness, or anything of that sort, so that he is permanently unable to discharge his duties as judge ; it does seem to me that in such a case as that he should be permitted to retire with his full salary. If the principle is good in one case it would seem to me that it is good in the other case. Indeed there might be far stronger reasons why in the case I speak of he should be retired with his full salary than in the other case. If a man goes on the bench at 45 and leaves his practice, and then at 50 years of age, after his practice has gone from him, he is unfit by infirmity to sit upon the bench, he has either to do one thing or the other, he has to retire on two-thirds of his income-and that is impossible in our province, where the judges have only $4,000 a year-or else he has to remain on the bench and not discharge his duties. It would be better in the public interest to allow a judge who has been in service five or ten years and becomes permanently afflicted, to retire on full salary.

One strong argument to support the ground that in case of infirmity a judge should retire and retain his full salary, is that a judge should at once, when he finds himself unable to discharge his duties, be in a position to retire. I know one instance where a judge would retire now, but because of the fact that he cannot retire with his full salary he does not feel in a position to retire, and, therefore, the administration of justice is retarded by the presence of a judge who ought not to discharge judicial duties on account of his infirmity, and who would not discharge them if he had an opportunity of retiring on full pay. When there is a physical infirmity rendering a judge incapable of fulfilling his duties, I think he should be allowed to retire on full salary, in order that whenever he feels that he is not capable of exercising his duties, properly, he can step down and out without financial regret.
I want to say one word in support of the views of the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Galliher). I think the salary of $2,400 a year for the county court judges of Nova Septia is entirely inadequate at the present time. When the salaries were fixed twenty years ago. there might have been something to be said in favour of such a small figure ; but to-day that salary is utterly inadequate to enable a judge to maintain that social position which is necessary to the proper dignity

of a judge. It is so small that it rather renders him an object of sympathy and pity than of dignity. That should not be the case. Our judges should be in a position to live well and to be independent of any thought of dependence on the public or otherwise.
Then, I have often been anxious, even before I entered this parliament, to bring another matter to the notice of the Minister of Justice and the other lawyers in this House. At confederation there was a principle established of making a distinction in the salaries of the judges in the different provinces according to the population or the area of those provinces. I think that distinction is absolutely vicious. If a judge in British Columbia, where the population may be only 300,000, exercises the highest judicial functions in that province, on whati ground of justice is he paid a smaller salary than the judge who exercises the same ljigh functions in another province, simply because the territory or the population happens to be smaller ? I regard this as a most invidious and unjust distinction. In fact, it makes a judge of the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia Inferior to a judge of the High Court or to a judge who exercises similar jurisdiction in some other province. If a judge exercises supreme jurisdiction in his province, whether it is over twenty people or over one million, his salary should be equal to that of any judge in Ontario or Quebec. After all, it makes no difference in principle that the population is larger in one province than it is in another, because the judge can only do so much work in the province. As a matter of fact, the judicial territory in the larger provinces is divided up, so that a judge in a judicial district in Ontario or Quebec has no! more population or territory to exercise jurisdiction over than a judge in Prince Edward Island. Although the province is larger, the particular district to which the labours of the judge are confined is not in many instances as large as the circuit in the smaller provinces. Therefore I ask the hon. Minister of Justice to wipe out this unjust and invidious distinction, introduced at the time of confederation. I think all the legal gentlemen in this House will support me in the contention that there is no reason why the salary of a superior court judge in Ontario should be one cent more than the salary of a superior court judge in British Columbia, Prince Edward Island or Nova Scotia. Judges exercising similar jurisdiction in every part of Canada should be paid the same salaries. I say that in defence of the judges of Nova Scotia, and I am sure that every legal gentleman from everjr other province will assert the same principle.

The difference in the salaries of the judges in the different provinces has been a standing grievance for a long time, and I trust that 254i
at no very distant day something may be done in the direction of levelling up judicial salaries. However, one must not try to do too much at one time, and if I accomplish now what I have undertaken, I think I shall accomplish something, and I would prefer to leave another part of the work to some future time.

I would like to ask the Minister of Justice a question or two in regard to the demeanour of judges towards gentlemen at the bar and court-houses full of ratepayers. I have not much to say of a derogatory nature of the judges of the province of Nova Scotia. I have always understood that most of these gentlemen have been men of great learning, of high character and generally of gentlemanly demeanour. But I wish to bring before the notice of the Minister cf Justice the fact that on two or three occasions during the last year or two the bar has been subjected to indignities by members of the bench and court-houses crowded with respectable ratepayers have been attacked in the most malignant way by one or more judges of the province of Nova Scotia. I ask, is a judge within his rights when he reflects on the character of a committee appointed by a county council to contract a court-house ? Is he within his right when he makes a malignant attack on the tastes of a court-house filled with well-behaved ratepayers ? I will not say more than this, but I hope this reference will secure in the future more respectful treatment of lawyers and of people whose business of inclination takes them to a courthouse. I would intimate to these judges, if my remarks should reach their ears, that if they wish to command the dignity due them, they must treat barristers and the people who frequent their courts with that consideration to which they are entitled.

Being a layman, I had no intention of taking part in this discussion, but I certainly consider that I would be derelict in my duty to my county were I to remain silent. The resolutions with regard to the pensions of judges are, to my mind, contrary to what I consider a just principle. Our judges in our different courts are supposed to live within their salaries, but if they are improvident and lay nothing by for a rainy day, that is their own faults and they should suffer the consequences. I would very much rather increase the salaries of our judges than give them pensions. We have more judges now than we have work for, if I can judge by the work of my own county. There the judges sit twice a year and despatch the business in two or three days. I therefore do not see why the number should not be reduced by one-half, and then give double pay to the others and abolish this system of pensions. The public who have to pay the judges' salaries and pensions are deserving of some consideration. In my opin-

ion, the principle of pensions to any one, I care not who he may be, is wrong, and I take this opportunity of expressing my disapproval of so uncalled for, extravagant and unprecedented a drain as calls, on the exchequer of this country.
On resolution 2,
That seems to be very exceptional treatment.

We will let that stand and consider it another time.
On resolution 3,

I was somewhat surprised to find that the lion. Minister of Justice had made some changes in the ages at which county court judges may be compulsorily retired. When this resolution was first put on the Order paper, it read, ' seventy-five years,' but now it is ' eighty.' I am of the opinion that not one man in eighty is as capable las younger men. I have made some inquiries, and have failed to find a mercantile or financial institution in this country with a man as manager at the age of eighty. Let a man seventy years old seek employment in any institution where brainwork is required, and he will not in many cases succeed, but even should his application be entertained, the undertaking would not prosper under his management as it would under the management of a younger man. I consider the position of county court judge a very responsible one-one that requires a man to be in possession of all his faculties. This is certainly required of a man who has to look into and decide intricate cases, and that generally without delay. Besides that the position is a responsible one, for the. reason that from the decisions of a county court judge, in many cases, there is no appeal. Look at the case from a merchant's standpoint. A merchant may sue a man for 8100 or $200; and if the judge is incapable of giving a proper decision, he not only injures that merchant from a monetary point of view, but his character as well. I propose therefore to move in amendment to clause 3 that the word ' eighty ' be struck out in the first line, and ' seventy-five ' be substituted, and that ' seventy-five ' be struck out in the third line and ' seventy ' be substituted.

The reason for the change from seventy-five to eighty is this. When the resolutions were first introduced they attracted some attention, and I discovered that in Ontario there were three county court judges who would be compulsorily retired at seventy-five, notwithstanding the fact that they had not served twenty-five years. Consequently, they would have been obliged to retire on two-thirds their salary. Under the circumstances, I thought it better to extend the period of time into eighty. The law Mr. KAULBACH.
now provides for action by the executive where you have a county court judge not competent to perform his duties. An application may be made to the Minister of Justice, and he can appoint a commissioner who will hold an investigation, and the judge may be retired by Order in Council. So that we have that provision at the present time, and I think it is only fair to go as far as we can towards giving such relief to the county court judges as we can give; and I do not think we are giving too much by adopting the resolution in its present form.

The rule of forcing retirement on the county court judges is, no doubt a very harsh rule. I do not know whether the Minister of Justice has gone so far as to say that he would have that made compulsory with the Superior Court judges, if he had the authority to do so. I think that when an hon. gentleman brings a resolution in this House, he ought to have the courage to make a charge rather than shelter himself behind the privileges of parliament. The hon. member for Kent (Mr. Stephens) insinuates, without having the courage to state and take the responsibility of his statement, that one of the county court judges, presumably in the county he represents, is unfit for his position. Will the hon. gentleman declare from his place in this House that there is a county court judge in the county of Kent who is unfit to discharge his duties ? If he is prepared to do that he will assume some responsibility and will show some courage. This is not the first time the hon. gentleman has played a second part in these matters. The hon. gentleman some time ago proposed a resolution in this House which he had never framed, a word of which he had never written, but which had been placed in his hands, with regard to one of the Superior Court judges. He is now playing an equally false part with regard to his own county. He has had a resolution placed in his hands to move here, prompted by somebody from his riding who wants to secure an appointment there. If he wishes to make a charge against the county of Kent judges let him be man enough to make that charge rather than insinuate what he dare not state.

I may tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) that he is mistaken in saying that this resolution was written out and given to me. It is wholly my own suggestion. And I was not making any insinuation as to the judge of the county court in Kent county. I simply say that there are several judges that I know of in Canada who are not capable of discharging their duties.	.
How does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Stephens) know that ?
I know it from statements made to me by solicitors in the different counties.
What counties ?

There is no need to say what counties. The hon. gentleman from Bothweil (Mr. Clancy) is wrong when he insinuates that this amendment was placed in my hands to be read to the House. He evidently thinks that there is no one capable of doing anything in this House except himself. In that he makes a sad mistake. Beyond the age limit I have proposed, very few men are able to discharge the diities of any bench, to say nothing of the county court bench. A judge of the county court has great responsibility. He is only one man, and in many case?, there is no appeal from his decision. His position is more important than that of a judge of a higher court.
Will the hon. gentleman state what hardships have come under his notice to induce him to take the course he does ?

It is not necessary that I should state them. I say that a man of eighty years of age is not capable of discharging properly the duties of a judge. I think that is a good stand, and that is the stand I am going to take.

The hon. gentleman, I think, stated that I thought nobody to be capable of doing certain things except myself. I wish to say that I do not think there is any gentleman in this House capable of doing what he has done except himself.
Oh, oh.
I wish to say to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) who gives vent to that utterance that he is not playing a part consistent with the high position he holds as a member of the legal profession.
I am not a judge.

Surely the hon. gentleman ought to stand by the eminent members of his own profession who are guilty of no greater crime than that of growing old, I hope he will be spared to be as guilty as the oldest of them, and that nobody will say ' oh ! ' when that time comes should his case be discussed. I do not expect to see that time myself. As to the hon. member for Kent, he is not a legal gentleman. Depending upon hearsay and that, no doubt, from some person who wishes to get an appointment at his hands, he comes to this House and, partly insinuates that certain judges are unfit to occupy their position at eighty years of age, yet refuses' to state that he knows of a single case where hardship has arisen from cases of that kind. I think I can leave him in the position he occupies, a position which does not display great courage.
Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) know of any judge who is not capable of discharging his duties ?
I have never said that there was one.
But does the hon. gentleman know of any such case ?
I know of none.
May I ask the Minister of Justice how many judges in Ontario will be retired under this Bill if it passes as he proposes ?

The committee will be surprised to learn how few judges will be given relief under these resolutions, should they pass in their entirety, in the High Court there are only two men in the whole province of Quebec, one man in Nova Scotia, and one in the North-west Territories.
Who is in Nova Scotia ?

The chief justice, who is seventy-five years of age and has been twenty-two years on the bench. There is one man, Judge Richardson in the North-west Territories. In New Brunswick there is one, the chief justice. With respect to the county court judges in the county courts of Ontario, there are Judge Elliot, who is eighty years of age and lias been thirty-four years on the bench; Judge Hughes eighty-one years of age and forty-eight years on the bench; Judge Deacon, seventy-nine years of age and thirty-five years and six months on the bench; Judge Lazier, seventy six years of age and twenty-one and one-half years on the bench; Judge O'Brien, eighty-three years of age and thirteen and one-half years on the bench; Judge Ketclium, seventy-five years and six months of age, and fourteen and one-half years on the bench; Judge Woods, eighty-four years of age, and seventeen and one-haif years on the bench. In the county court of New Brunswick there is Judge Stevens, who is eighty-one years of age and who has been thirty-six years on the bench-and who, I may say, has been for a long time asking for such legislation-as is now brought in.
Has the hon. minister any account or memorandum as to the number who would be retired in the course of two or three years.

No. It took considerable time and labour to get together the information for this memorandum. Unfortunately we have not in the department the ages of the judges at the term of their appointment and have some difficulty in ascertaining them. I do not apprehend that there are very many who would be affected by this legislation within the next two or three years.
The hon. minister will not be able to find out their ages now.

I may say that I have not had any complaint with respect to the legislation now proposed. I

do not think its operation will produce hardship. After all, judges who have got beyond seventy-five years of age retire with full pension. So, there is no hardship so far as they are concerned.
They ought to have full pension.
Some of them ought.
In regard to Judge Deacon's age, he is in his 81st year, instead of 79.
I have taken Judge Deacon's word for it.
I have taken Judge Deacon's word for it myself, within the last three months.

In view of the prospect of three more appointments of county court judges in the province of Ontario, I think the Minister of Justice might give a thought as to how these appointments shall be made. A principle was inaugurated in the province of Ontario that worked out well, namely that it was thought better not to bring active politicians from the scenes of their fights and place them on the bench. That principle was observed by Sir John Thompson, and was supposed to be an admirable one, but owing to party exigencies the Minister of Justice, since he has been in office, has been forced to break in upon it, and the result is that we see in the province of Ontario, installed in judicial places, men who have been the keenest politicians and are now brought face to face with the people with whom they have been fighting for many years. While that has been going on, I must congratulate the Minister of Justice that in the county of York, and in the county of Grey, he did not promote the junior judges. I think that was an admirable conclusion arrived at by the minister. I think that both those gentlemen who are junior judges deserve richly to be reprimanded as they were by not being promoted. I hope the active part taken by them in politics will be a lesson to all junior judges in future, and that they will prefer to take chances of preferment by reason of their merits rather than by reason of their political affiliations. Coming down to the question before us, I say that in my opinion the salaries of Superior Court judges, particularly in Ontario, are notj liigh enough. I wish to say also that I think there are too many judges in our province. What have we seen lately '! At the last session of the Ontario legislature, in deference to political, leverage, for it cannot be anything else, the provincial government has arranged for the appointment practically of three more judges. As I understand the law, once the province has determined upon the appointments, then it is the duty of the federal power to supply the salaries. It is a notorious fact that in Ontario the superior court judges are not Hon. Mr. FITZPATRICK.
pressed with work. I think perhaps there has been some congestion so far as appeal judges go.
Mr. McCarthy. Is it not a fact that there are only two judges to be appointed, and one is to be taken from the chancery division ?

That will be two too many, in the opinion of the general public, I think. It comes to this, that in the province of Ontario we all believe that we should have better men on the bench than some of the gentlemen who have been getting' on. In order to get the best men, you have got to pay higher salaries. 1 have understood that there are Superior-Court judges to-day in the province of Ontario who are quite willing to do more work, but they expect more pay for it, and I think they are right. It is a notorious fact that in past years Superior Court judges in Ontario have crippled the courts, owing to the fact that they were absent from their duties. In regard to county court judges, it has got to be a screaming farce, appointments are made in counties where there is no more need for a junior judge than there is for five wheels to a wagon. I am not going to say that the government who are now in power are entirely to blame for that, because I think the former government erred in that respect also. But now that there is to be an appointment in the county of Prescott, let me draw the attention of the Minister of Justice to the fact that in that county last year there was not a single case tried in the so-called county court. There might harm been a division court case, but the return shows that in the county of Prescott not a single case was. tried before the county court. In view of that fact, and seeing there is a junior judge in that county, it would be well to promote him, and in that way do away with one. Take the county of Ontario, which has two judges, in that county last year there were three cases tried. Political exigencies have played such a part in the appointment of judges that we find in the county of Ontario that Judge McCrimmon, the senior judge, is a man in the prime of life, and yet lie is as-isted by a junior judge, and owing to political exigencies it was found necessary to appoint a third gentleman as surrogate court judge. So there are three gentlemen practically standing around to do work that might be done by one. The time has arrived when there should be a thorough revolution in relation to county court judges. Let there be fewer of them. So far as salaries go, I think, with the addition of the surrogate fees that are paid to them, their salaries are fairly good ; but in regard to the superior court judges, I think it is the opinion of the lawyers and of the general public that they should be paid higher salaries and that there should be fewer of them.

My hon. friend is somewhat mistaken when he says that Sir John Thompson laid down the principle that county court judges should be taken from the bar outside the district to which they were appointed. That principle was laid down by him, it is true, but when the question came up for discussion some time ago in the House, I had an analysis made of the appointments that were made by Sir John Thompson, and when this resolution comes up again for consideration I intend to bring that 'down, and the hon. gentlemen will learn that we have all sinned very much with respect to these appointments. While the rule has been laid down by Sir John Thompson, I am not disposed to say that I think that rule ought to be abrogated.
I would like to ask the Minister of Justice whether this clause is intended to affect junior court judges as well as county court judges.
Ail county court judges.

It says every county court judge. In some legislation that took place a few years ago with regard to the salaries of county court judges, that expression was used, and it was afterwards construed to have application only to senior judges, but not to junior judges. I would suggest to the hon. minister that that be made perfectly clear by adding junior judges. While I am on my feet, I desire to say a word with reference to the salaries that are paid to county court judges. I quite agree with the remarks that have been made by some hon. members that the county court judges are not sufficiently paid. As I understand the matter, the salaries now paid to county court judges were fixed at the time of confederation and there has been no increase since then. But there has been a decrease of some $200 to $400. At the time the salaries were fixed, it is an actual fact that the cost of living to a county court judge was very much less than it is at the present time. The salary was then fixed, not only having regard to the cheapness of living, but having regard to the duties that were then expected to be performed by a county court judge. Now while there has been no increase in the salary there has been a very significant increase in the cost living of the county court judges and there has been a very significant increase in the am unt of work they are expected to perform. Instead of only performing the duties belonging to county courts and division courts, as they were intended to perform at the time of confederation, there has been passed since that time not less than 52 Ontario and Dominion statutes, imposing additional duties upon county court judges. Now, is it reasonable to expect that they should perform the duties imposed upon them by these 52 additional Acts of parliament without additional salary, while at the same time they are obliged to pay a higher cost for living than at the time their salaries were fixed. In fact they are paid a smaller sum.
It does appear to me that it is entirely unfair to the county court judges. This matter was recognized by parliament in regard to the superior court judges, when in 1873 an Act was passed Increasing the salaries of the high court judges it was put in the preamble, that owing to the increased cost of living, the government of the day felt it incumbent upon themselves to increase the salaries of the superior court judges. If there was an increase in the cost of living for the superior court judges, there was a similar increase in the cost of living for the county court judges and while parliament increased the salaries of the sup-perior court judges it decreased the salaries of the county court judges. There is another very cogent reason why the salaries of the county court judges should be increased. A part of the means of adding to their salaries has been taken away from them. In former times it was quite the usual practice for a county court judge to fill the dual position of county court judge and local master of the high court. Now, in any county of this province where that position becomes vacant it is no longer given to the county court judge, but an appointment from the bar is made to fill that position and that source of revenue is cut oft' from the county court judge. In former days fees that were derivable from the business transacted in the surrogate court were given to the county court judges, but now the practice is that if that position becomes vacant a special appointment is made from the bar to fill the position and these fees go into the pocket of the appointee and are not received by the county court judge. One other strong reason why county court judges should be paid more is this':	County court judges,
in addition to being county court judges, are to all intents and purposes superior court judges with the one single exception that they do not try high court cases, but all chamber motions and applications of all sorts In connection with cases in their respective counties are heard by the county court judges as local judges of the high court and instead of this business being performed by the judges of the high court in Toronto as formerly.it is now performed by the judges of the county court and in that way their duties have been very materially increased, while there has been no proper adjustment of their salaries. If I understood correctly we have received an intimation from the Minister of Justice that something would be done in the future for these county court judges and I hope he will see his way clear to do something for them in the very near future.

I entirely agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Hastings

(Mr. Porter) as to the necessity of increasing the salaries paid to county court judges on account of the additional cost of living at the present time as compared with that at the time their salaries were fixed and the additional duties that they have to perform. In my own province we are not so fortunate as to have one or two judges for a single county. We have only one judge to attend to the judicial duties in several counties and that statute respecting speedy trials has caused a very large increase in the expenses of the judges. The judge of the county that I represent is also the judge of the county of Albert. If a man is charged with a criminal offence the judge is obliged to go to the county of Albert when this person applies for trial, and he is put to considerable expense for railway fare and also his living expenses during the time' he is absent. For this he receives no remuneration whatever. I think the salaries of the county court judges should be increased for the reasons which have been so ably enumerated by the hon. member for Hastings.

I have a great deal of sympathy with what has been said by the hon. member for West Hastings (Mr. Porter) in regard to an increase in the salaries of the county court judges and I would like to repeat what I said before, that I concur in the statement that our county court judges should be better paid, but I am afraid I am placed in the same position that much more eminent men than myself have found themselves in when they attempted to increase the salaries of the county court judges. They withdrew the resolutions after they had got them into committee. This question has been under consideration since 1888. I have a letter written by Sir John Thompson to one of the judges, in which he says that he hopes during that session to bring down a resolution for the purpose of increasing the salaries of the judges of the high court and the county courts. Unfortunately, he never got beyond the resolution. I think the judges are not paid sufiictently well. I think they ought to receive further consideration, but, however, that is only my own personal view and I cannot do more than express it.

I desire to say a word in reference to the controversy that took place between the hon. Minister of Justice and the hon. member for East Sim-coe (Mr. Bennett) in reference to the policy laid down by the late Sir John Thompson.
I remember quite well, when Sir John Thompson was Minister of Justice, pressing him to make an appointment' in my own county and he informed me that he had determined upon the line of policy intimated by the hon. member for East Simcoe and that he could not make the appointment of the gentleman we then thought It desirable to appoint, and he did

not make it. Might I suggest that the hon. member for East Simcoe is quite correct and at the same time the hon. Minister of Justice may be correct? Posibly at the commencement of his term of office Sir John Thompson had not adopted that policy, but after having been Minister of Justice for one or two years he came to the conclusion that it was a proper policy to adopt and that from that time forward he did adhere to that policy. The hon. Minister of Justice may be quite correct in saying that he made appointments in a way different from that intimated by the hon. member for East Simcoe, but these appointments may have been made in the earlier part of the regime of Sir John Thompson.

I will produce here a list of the names of the gentlemen appointed, the districts to which they were appointed and the dates at which they were appointed. I have a memo, all prepared and I will have it here when these resolutions are taken up again.
It occurred to me that both the hon. gentlemen were right.

Could the hon. Minister of Justice give us some data as to the judges who will be affected by this eighty year provision. I understand that the amendment proposes that the word ' eighty ' shall be struck out and that ' seventy-five ' shall be substituted.

I think it is a pity that the hon. Minister of Justice did not have sufficient courage, as his predecessor had, to bring down a resolution to increase the salaries of the county court judges and let us see who are the members of this committee who will stand up and say that thev are sufficiently paid. I can only speak of the province of Ontario, and I am bound to say that I do not think there is any man in the public service that is as poorly paid as the ordinary county court judge in that province. It is no criterion of the work of a county court judge, when you speak of the number of cases that are returned as having been tried in the county court. In that return there are only included certain cases over which the judge has civil jurisdiction. To begin with, the county court judge saves the country an enormous amount of expense in the trying of criminals. More and more every day men charged with criminal offences are advised by their counsel that they are just as safe in trusting their liberties to the county court judges as to a jury. I am safe in saying that two-thirds of those charged with criminal offences in nearly every county of Ontario now elect to be tried by the county court judges, and the county court judge's have power to try all offences except murder or treason. It must be recognized by parliament that judges who have such full jurisdiction in regard to the liberties of the

subject, must be competent men or else tlie parliament of Canada would not allow them to do that work. Considering tlie cost of living to-day, and considering that a public servant who is underpaid is not fairly treated, we have, I think, to admit that our county court judges are not treated by the country as they should be. I wonder sometimes that we can get competent men to take the position, and I often think that it must be public spirit rather than the salary that induces them to do so. Probably they desire to se*rve their country rather than to look to the compensation that attaches to the office. I know that many county court judges could not live on the salaries they get had they not private means. That ought not be so. If a man has not got a shilling and yet is fit to be a county court judge, the salary ought to be sufficient to enable him to take the office. Without unduly delaying the House at this late hour, I wish to emphasize particularly on the Minister of Justice that had he brought down a resolution to increase the salaries of the county court judges-I speak of those in the province of Ontario about whom I am most competent to speak-such a resolution would have received the support of a large majority of the members of this House. I regret that the Minister of Justice did not bring down such a resolution, because I believe that the county court judges in Ontario at least are at present very much underpaid.

The amendment proposes to reduce the age of compulsory retirement from 80 years to 75 years, it being 75 years in the original resolution. I believe for the reasons given by the Minister of Justice, that the age should be maintained at 80. It would work a great hardship on several of the county court judges if the age is not so maintained. In my county the judge who on his appointment had every reason to believe that he would be continued during life and good behaviour in his office, will be about 23 years on the bench when he is 75 years old. That would only entitle him to two-thirds of his allowance, and I believe that would be unfair. Several such cases occur in Ontario, and I believe that 80 years should be maintained as the age of compulsory retirement.
What period of years does the Minister of Justice intend to insert in the blank?
I do not intend putting the resolution through to-night, and I thought I would like to hear what the committee had to say on the subject. I shall take it into further consideration.
What is the reason for confining it to a certain number of years?

That was inserted when we had the limit fixed
at 75, but now in view of the change I do not think there is any need for it now.
Amendment allowed to stand.
On section 4,
I wish to amend section 4 by striking out the figures ' thirty-five' in the second line and substituting the word ' thirty ' therefor.

Why have you fix any number of years here? I do not see why, if a county court judge becomes afflicted with some permanent disability 25 years or 20 years or even 10 years after he has been appointed to office, he should not be taken care of by the state just as well as after 35 years. I cannot see any merit in a man having the good luck to be in office a few years longer before lie was afflicted with some permanent infirmity. If it is a sudden affliction that comes to a man it is a matter he cannot control. If a man having given up his profession and not intending to retire, but being rendered by the act of God afflicted so that he cannot perform his duties, it seems to me he ought to have the right to be looked after no matter at what period of his service it happens. _

My hon. friend will remember that up to last year or the year before if a county court judge became permanently disabled at any time before he had been on the bench for ten years, be simply went off and got nothingat all. Last year the lavy was amended so that if he had served five years he became entitled to half his pay, and if he had served ten years to two-thirds of his pay. If we did make this change with respect to tlie county court judges, we would put them in a more favourable position than the high court judges ?
That might not be undesirable, considering the small salaries they get.
Suppose a judge is not willing to resign his office, what does the lion. Minister of Justice propose to do ?

That is a serious question. We had two cases of that kind in Canada, and in neither case was anything done except to let the judge continue on. That has been the course followed in England. I would ask my hon. friend to let the amendment stand as well as the resolution, and I would ask that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.
Progress reported.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved the adjournment of the House.
What will be the order of business to-morrow ?

The Railway Commission Bill will be taken up, and we will endeavour to clear off other matters on the Order Paper as much as possible, probably the lead resolutions, and later in the day other Bills may possibly be dealt with.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 12.30 a.m., Thursday.
